chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region

questions.text: For each term in the left column, choose the appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: A ganglion is a collection of cell bodies outside the CNS. A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers within the CNS. A nucleus is a collection of cell bodies within the CNS. A lemniscus is a collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibers outside the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Ganglion = peripheral cell bodies; nucleus = central cell bodies; tract/lemniscus = CNS fiber bundles

pairs.target: A collection of cell bodies outside CNS
A bundle of nerve fibers within CNS
A collection of cell bodies within CNS
A collection of ascending fibers within brain stem
A bundle of nerve fibers outside CNS

questions.text: The nucleus is:
questions.explanation: A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies within the CNS. A ganglion is the equivalent in the PNS. Nerve fibers form tracts or nerves, not nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus = cluster of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS
options: A group of cell bodies within peripheral nervous system.
A group of cell bodies within central nervous system.
A group of nerve fibers within peripheral nervous system.
A group of nerve fibers within central nervous system.
A collection of nerve fibers in brain stem.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers within the CNS. A pathway is a chain of successive tracts with the same function. A lemniscus is a collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem. Afferent means input toward a structure. A ganglion is a group of cell bodies outside the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Tract = CNS fiber bundle; pathway = chain of tracts; lemniscus = ascending brainstem fibers
options: Ganglion – a group of cell bodies within CNS.
Pathway – a chain of successive tracts having different functions.
Lemniscus – a collection of descending fibers within the brain stem.
Afferent – an output going away from a certain structure.
Tract – a bundle of nerve fibers within CNS.

questions.text: A chain of successive tracts in CNS having the same function is called:
questions.explanation: A pathway is a chain of successive tracts in the CNS serving the same function. A fasciculus is a smaller bundle within a tract. A lemniscus is a specific ascending brainstem pathway. A commissure connects two sides of the CNS, and a decussation is a midline crossing.
questions.keyConcept: Pathway = chain of successive tracts with identical function

questions.text: A bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS having the same beginning, termination and function is called:
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS sharing the same origin, termination, and function. A pathway is a chain of tracts. A lemniscus is an ascending brainstem bundle. A commissure connects hemispheres, and a decussation is a crossing.
questions.keyConcept: Tract = CNS fiber bundle with common origin, termination, and function

questions.text: The lowermost soft part of the auricle of ear is called:
questions.explanation: The lobule is the soft, fleshy lower part of the auricle (earlobe). The tragus is the small pointed projection anterior to the ear canal. The concha is the bowl-shaped depression.
questions.keyConcept: Lobule = soft lower part of the auricle (earlobe)

questions.text: Pain from upper lip is carried by:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve, a terminal branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2), exits through the infraorbital foramen to supply skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the upper lip

questions.text: Sensation from the angle of mandible is carried by:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the temple and anterior auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve supplies skin over the angle of the mandible

questions.text: The nerve that carries the sensation for the lower eyelid is:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. The supraorbital nerve (V1) supplies the upper eyelid and forehead.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) carries sensation from the lower eyelid

questions.text: Tumor from central part of upper lip would likely spread to which group of lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: The central part of the upper lip drains primarily to the submandibular lymph nodes. The upper lip also drains to the submental nodes via lymphatic crossing. The buccal and parotid nodes drain more lateral facial regions.
questions.keyConcept: Central upper lip drains to submandibular lymph nodes

questions.text: Pain from ala of nose is carried by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The ala of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) laterally and the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (V1) at the tip.
questions.keyConcept: Ala of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) and external nasal nerve (V1)

questions.text: The non-hairy region of the temple is supplied by which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: The zygomaticotemporal branch of the zygomatic nerve (V2) supplies the non-hairy skin of the temple region. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp of the temple.
questions.keyConcept: Zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the non-hairy temple region

questions.text: Loss of sensation from lower eye lid indicates injury of:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) exits through the infraorbital foramen and supplies the skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. Loss of sensation indicates injury to this nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower eyelid skin

questions.text: Which one of the following scalp nerves is derived from dorsal rami of spinal nerves?
questions.explanation: The greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of C2. It supplies the skin of the occipital region of the scalp. The auriculotemporal, great auricular, lesser occipital, and posterior auricular nerves are ventral ramus derivatives.
questions.keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve = dorsal ramus of C2

questions.text: The artery that lies above parotid duct is a direct branch of:
questions.explanation: The transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery (external carotid), runs above the parotid duct. The facial artery enters the face at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse facial artery lies above the parotid duct

questions.text: A 45-years-old woman is suffering from numbness over the tip of her nose. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be damaged?
questions.explanation: The tip of the nose is supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (ophthalmic division, V1). Therefore, numbness suggests damage to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Tip of the nose sensation = ophthalmic division (V1) via external nasal branch
options: Anterior division of the mandibular nerve
Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve

questions.text: The branch of the mandibular nerve that supplies the scalp is the:
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, supplies the scalp in the temporal region and the skin over the anterior auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp via the temporal region

questions.text: Infection of lateral part of the upper eye lid leads to enlargement of which group of lymph nodes:
questions.explanation: The lateral part of the upper eyelid drains to the parotid (pre-auricular) lymph nodes. The medial part drains to the submandibular nodes.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral upper eyelid drains to parotid lymph nodes

questions.text: The nerve supplying the buccinator muscle is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), specifically via its buccal branches. Although it is in the region of the mandibular nerve, the motor supply is from the facial nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII)

questions.text: The 2 frontal bellies:
questions.explanation: The two frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle originate from the skin of the eyebrows and interdigitate with the orbicularis oculi. They are not attached to the superior temporal line.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal bellies of occipitofrontalis originate from skin of eyebrows
options: Form the only muscle of face.
Are attached to superior temporal line.

questions.text: Which of the following is sensory to the scalp behind the auricle?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland, and the scalp behind the auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies scalp behind the auricle

questions.text: Retromandibular vein:
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the maxillary and superficial temporal veins. It begins inside the parotid gland, is deep to the facial nerve, and divides into anterior and posterior branches.
questions.keyConcept: Retromandibular vein = maxillary + superficial temporal; lies deep to facial nerve in parotid
options: Is formed by union of maxillary & superficial temporal veins.
Is deep to facial nerve inside parotid gland.

questions.text: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi:
questions.explanation: The lacrimal part of the orbicularis oculi is attached to the lacrimal sac and the posterior lacrimal crest. It helps drain tears by compression of the lacrimal sac.
questions.keyConcept: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attaches to lacrimal sac and aids tear drainage
options: Is attached to medial palpebral ligament.
Is attached to lateral palpebral raphe.
Is a part of orbicularis oris.

questions.text: Orbicularis oris originates from:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle originates from the modiolus (a fibromuscular condensation at the angle of the mouth) and inserts into the lips. It acts as the sphincter of the mouth.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oris originates from the modiolus

questions.text: Mandibular nerve is sensory to:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) carries sensation from the lower lip (via the mental nerve), chin, temporal region, and anterior ear. It does not supply the upper eyelid, lower eyelid, or tip of the nose.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve (V3) sensory supply includes the lower lip and chin

questions.text: Facial artery:
questions.explanation: The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery. It has a tortuous course to accommodate jaw movements and ends at the medial angle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery has a tortuous course and anastomoses with ophthalmic branches at the medial eye angle
options: Is a branch of internal carotid artery.
Enters face at antero-inferior angle of Buccinator.
Ends by anastomosing with supraorbital artery.

questions.text: Pulse felt at antero-inferior angle of masseter is from which artery?
questions.explanation: The facial artery can be palpated as it crosses the lower border of the mandible at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery pulse is palpable at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter

questions.text: Pain from capsule of parotid gland is carried by:
questions.explanation: The parotid capsule is innervated by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3), which carries pain fibers from the gland capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Parotid capsule pain is carried by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3)

questions.text: Bleeding in which layer of scalp causes black eye?
questions.explanation: Bleeding into the loose areolar connective tissue layer of the scalp allows blood to spread freely and gravitate into the eyelids via the subaponeurotic space, causing a black eye.
questions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue layer bleeding causes black eye via gravitational spread

questions.text: As regards scalp, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The scalp has numerous sebaceous glands associated with hair follicles. Its rich vascularity means wounds bleed profusely, and aponeurotic wounds gape due to muscle pull.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp has abundant sebaceous glands; wounds bleed profusely and gape if aponeurosis is cut
options: Its wounds gap if aponeurosis is cut.
Its veins communicate with intracranial venous sinuses.
It contains a muscle of facial expression.

questions.text: In which of the following layers of scalp does infection tend to spread?
questions.explanation: Infection spreads most readily in the loose areolar connective tissue layer because it contains valveless emissary veins that can transmit infection intracranially.
questions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue is the dangerous layer of the scalp due to valveless emissary veins

questions.text: The plane of movement of scalp is between:
questions.explanation: The scalp moves as a single unit because the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and epicranial aponeurosis are firmly attached. The plane of movement is between the epicranial aponeurosis and the pericranium.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp movement occurs between epicranial aponeurosis and pericranium

questions.text: The large blood vessels of scalp run in:
questions.explanation: The large blood vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer, which is richly vascularized and innervated.
questions.keyConcept: Blood vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer

questions.text: The nerve supply of the muscle of the sclap is:
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), specifically the temporal and posterior auricular branches. The great auricular and great occipital nerves are purely sensory.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII)

questions.text: The main sensory nerve of the upper lip is:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of maxillary division, V2) is the main sensory nerve of the upper lip, lower eyelid, and cheek.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) is the main sensory nerve of the upper lip

questions.text: The main sensory nerve of the lower lip is:
questions.explanation: The mental nerve, a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular division, V3), exits through the mental foramen to supply the skin of the lower lip and chin.
questions.keyConcept: Mental nerve (V3) is the main sensory nerve of the lower lip

questions.text: As regards orbicularis oculi muscle, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi has bony attachments both medially (medial palpebral ligament) and laterally (lateral palpebral raphe). Therefore, the statement that it has no medial bony attachment is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi has bony attachments medially and laterally
options: Its lacrimal part helps drainage of tears.
Its palpebral part closes the eye gently.
Its orbital part closes the eye tightly.
Its orbital part has no bony attachment medially.
Its palpebral part lies in the eyelids.

questions.text: Match the area of skin in left column with its corresponding nerve supply in the right column:
questions.explanation: Lateral upper eyelid → lacrimal nerve (V1). Tip of nose → external nasal nerve (V1). Lower lip → mental nerve (V3). Angle of mandible → great auricular nerve (C2–C3). Forehead → supraorbital nerve (V1).
questions.keyConcept: Specific facial skin areas have distinct sensory nerve supplies

questions.text: The pulse felt in front of tragus of ear against zygomatic arch is the pulse of:
questions.explanation: The superficial temporal artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid artery, can be palpated in front of the tragus of the ear against the zygomatic arch.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial temporal artery pulse is palpable anterior to the tragus against the zygomatic arch

questions.text: The Occipito-frontalis muscle:
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle elevates the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. The frontalis portion inserts into the epicranial aponeurosis.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis elevates the eyebrows

questions.text: Facial muscles:
questions.explanation: Facial muscles are sphincters and dilators of facial openings. They are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Facial muscles act as sphincters for facial orifices and are innervated by CN VII
options: Act as sphincters for facial openings.

questions.text: The muscle that causes firm closure of eyelids is:
questions.explanation: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi is responsible for firm (forced) closure of the eyelids. The palpebral part closes the eye gently.
questions.keyConcept: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi = forced eye closure; palpebral part = gentle closure

questions.text: Orbicularis oculi muscle:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. The levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) opens the eyelid.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids

questions.text: As regards buccinator muscle, all the following is true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII) via its buccal branches. It is NOT innervated by the mandibular nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the mandibular nerve
options: It is the muscle of the cheecks.
It arises from maxilla and mandible.
It is inserted in upper and lower lips.
It prevents accumulation of food in oral vestibule.
It is innervated by mandibular branch of trigeminal nerve.

questions.text: The sphincter of the lips is the:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris is the sphincter muscle of the lips. The buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oris = sphincter of the lips

questions.text: For each one of the layers of the scalp in left column, choose the appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: Skin = common site for sebaceous cysts. Epicranial aponeurosis = attached to superior temporal line. Loose connective tissue = dangerous layer. Pericranium = continuous with sutural ligaments. Dense connective tissue = wounds do not gape.
questions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue is the dangerous layer of the scalp due to emissary veins

pairs.target: Is attached to superior temporal line.
Considered as dangerous layer of scalp

questions.text: As regards the subcutaneous connective tissue layer of scalp, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous connective tissue layer of the scalp is dense and fibrous. Infections here are localized because the tissue is dense. Wounds bleed profusely because fibrous septa prevent vasoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Subcutaneous connective tissue of scalp is dense; infection is localized and wounds bleed profusely
options: It contains arteries & nerves of scalp.
It connects skin of scalp with aponeurosis of occipito-frontalis.

questions.text: As regards the occipital bellies of occipito-frontalis, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The two occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis are separated by the median tendinous intersection and take origin from the lateral two-thirds of the highest nuchal line.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital bellies originate from the highest nuchal line
options: They are separated by an extension of epicranial aponeurosis.
They take origin from epicranial aponeurosis.
They are inserted into lateral 2/3 of highest nuchal line.
They are supplied by temporal branch of facial nerve.

questions.text: Give an account on branches of facial artery in face. Describe the anastomosis in which it shares.
questions.explanation: The facial artery branches in the neck include ascending palatine, tonsillar, and glandular branches. In the face, it gives inferior labial, superior labial, and lateral nasal branches, ending as the angular artery. It anastomoses with the infraorbital branch of the maxillary artery, the transverse facial artery, and branches of the ophthalmic artery.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery anastomoses with ophthalmic, maxillary, and transverse facial branches
questions.modelAnswer: The facial artery gives off branches in the neck (ascending palatine, tonsillar, glandular) and in the face (inferior labial, superior labial, lateral nasal). It terminates as the angular artery at the medial angle of the eye. It anastomoses with the infraorbital branch of the maxillary artery, the transverse facial artery, and branches of the ophthalmic artery (supratrochlear, supraorbital).

questions.text: Enumerate the arteries of the scalp. Mention the origin of each artery.
questions.explanation: The arteries of the scalp include: (1) Supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries (from ophthalmic, internal carotid). (2) Superficial temporal artery (from external carotid). (3) Posterior auricular artery (from external carotid). (4) Occipital artery (from external carotid).
questions.keyConcept: Scalp arteries: supraorbital/trochlear (internal carotid), superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital (external carotid)
questions.modelAnswer: The arteries of the scalp are: (1) Supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries (branches of the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid). (2) Superficial temporal artery (terminal branch of the external carotid). (3) Posterior auricular artery (branch of the external carotid). (4) Occipital artery (branch of the external carotid). The supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries arise from the ophthalmic artery.

questions.text: Enumerate nerves of scalp in front of auricle.
questions.explanation: Nerves of the scalp in front of the auricle include: (1) Auriculotemporal nerve (V3). (2) Temporal branch of facial nerve (CN VII, motor). (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3). (4) Lesser occipital nerve (C2).
questions.keyConcept: Scalp nerves anterior to auricle: auriculotemporal (V3), temporal branch of facial nerve, great auricular (C2–3), lesser occipital (C2)
questions.modelAnswer: Nerves of the scalp in front of the auricle include: (1) Auriculotemporal nerve (branch of mandibular division V3), supplying the temporal region and anterior auricle. (2) Temporal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), motor to the frontalis. (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3), supplying the angle of the mandible and lower parotid region. (4) Lesser occipital nerve (C2), supplying the upper lateral neck.

questions.text: Enumerate nerves of scalp behind of auricle.
questions.explanation: Nerves of the scalp behind the auricle include: (1) Greater occipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C2). (2) Lesser occipital nerve (C2, ventral ramus). (3) Greater auricular nerve (C2–C3). (4) Posterior auricular nerve (CN VII, motor).
questions.keyConcept: Scalp nerves posterior to auricle: greater occipital (C2 dorsal), lesser occipital (C2 ventral), great auricular (C2–3), posterior auricular (CN VII)
questions.modelAnswer: Nerves of the scalp behind the auricle include: (1) Greater occipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C2), supplying the occipital scalp. (2) Lesser occipital nerve (ventral ramus of C2), supplying the upper lateral neck and lower lateral scalp. (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3), supplying the angle of the mandible. (4) Posterior auricular nerve (branch of CN VII), motor to the occipitalis and auricular muscles.

questions.text: Describe branches of Ophthalmic nerve that share in nerve supply of face.
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches into the lacrimal, frontal, and nasociliary nerves. The frontal nerve divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves, supplying the forehead and scalp. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral upper eyelid. The nasociliary nerve gives the infratrochlear nerve and anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches: lacrimal, frontal (supraorbital/supratrochlear), nasociliary
questions.modelAnswer: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) gives rise to the lacrimal, frontal, and nasociliary nerves. The frontal nerve divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves, supplying the forehead and scalp. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral part of the upper eyelid. The nasociliary nerve gives the infratrochlear nerve, anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves, and the long ciliary nerves.

questions.text: Describe branches of Maxillary nerve that share in nerve supply of face.
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives the zygomatic nerve (zygomaticotemporal and zygomaticofacial branches), the infraorbital nerve, and branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion. It exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve (V2) branches: zygomatic, infraorbital, pterygopalatine ganglion branches
questions.modelAnswer: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives the zygomatic nerve (which divides into zygomaticotemporal and zygomaticofacial branches), the infraorbital nerve (supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper lip), and branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion. It exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.

questions.text: Describe branches of Mandibular nerve that share in nerve supply of face.
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) has sensory branches including the buccal nerve (cheek), auriculotemporal nerve (temple), lingual nerve (tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (mental nerve for lower lip and chin). It exits via the foramen ovale.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve (V3) branches: buccal, auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar (mental)
questions.modelAnswer: The mandibular nerve (V3) has sensory branches including the buccal nerve (cheek skin and mucosa), auriculotemporal nerve (temple and anterior auricle), lingual nerve (anterior two-thirds of tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (which gives the mental nerve for the lower lip and chin). It exits the skull via the foramen ovale.

questions.text: Describe parts of orbicularis oculi muscle.
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi has three parts: (1) Orbital part: outer thick portion, forceful eye closure. (2) Palpebral part: thin portion in eyelids, gentle closure/blinking. (3) Lacrimal part: deep portion attached to lacrimal sac, aids tear drainage.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi parts: orbital (forced closure), palpebral (gentle closure), lacrimal (tear drainage)
questions.modelAnswer: The orbicularis oculi has three parts: (1) Orbital part: the outer thick portion attached to the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments; responsible for forceful eye closure. (2) Palpebral part: the thin portion in the eyelids; responsible for gentle closure (blinking). (3) Lacrimal part: the deep portion attached to the lacrimal sac; aids tear drainage via the lacrimal canaliculi.

questions.text: A D years old child fell off his bicycle & his head hit the pavement. A 2 cm long wound in his scalp was seen. Soon, he was sitting in a pool of blood.
questions.explanation: The scalp has a rich blood supply and dense connective tissue that prevents vessel constriction, leading to profuse bleeding. The dangerous layer is the loose areolar tissue because it contains valveless emissary veins.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp wounds bleed profusely due to rich vascularity and inability to constrict

subQuestions.text: Why does the scalp bleed profusely?
subQuestions.explanation: The dense fibrous septa in the scalp's subcutaneous layer tether the vessels open, preventing vasoconstriction and causing profuse bleeding.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Scalp dense fibrous tissue prevents vasoconstriction → profuse bleeding
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Because the scalp has a rich blood supply and the fibrous tissue in the connective tissue layer prevents the local vasoconstriction of the blood vessels in this layer.

subQuestions.text: Name the arteries that supply the scalp.
subQuestions.explanation: The scalp is supplied by five paired arteries: supraorbital and supratrochlear (internal carotid), and superficial temporal, posterior auricular, and occipital (external carotid).
subQuestions.keyConcept: Five arteries supply the scalp: supraorbital, supratrochlear, superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Arteries supplying the scalp in front of the auricle: supraorbital artery, supratrochlear artery, and superficial temporal artery. Behind the auricle: posterior auricular artery and occipital artery.

subQuestions.text: Which is the dangerous layer of the scalp? Why is it dangerous?
subQuestions.explanation: The loose areolar tissue contains valveless emissary veins that communicate with intracranial venous sinuses, allowing infection to spread intracranially.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue contains valveless emissary veins → intracranial spread
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Loose areolar tissue layer because it contains the emissary veins that are valveless and can take infection to the inside of the skull.

questions.text: L1 spinal cord segment lies at level of which one of following vertebra:
questions.explanation: In adults, the spinal cord ends at L1–L2, and the vertebral level is approximately 2–3 segments higher than the spinal cord segment at lower levels. The L1 cord segment lies at the T10 vertebral level.
questions.keyConcept: L1 spinal cord segment ≈ T10 vertebral level

questions.text: Compression of which segment of the spinal cord would occur by a tumor at 4th thoracic vertebra?
questions.explanation: There is a discrepancy between vertebral and spinal cord levels in the thoracic region. The spinal cord segments are approximately 2 levels higher than their corresponding vertebrae in the lower thoracic region. A tumor at T4 would compress the T6 spinal cord segment.
questions.keyConcept: Lower thoracic spinal cord segments are ~2 vertebral levels higher than the vertebrae

questions.text: At birth the spinal cord ends at the level of:
questions.explanation: At birth, the spinal cord extends to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Due to differential growth of the vertebral column, the cord ascends to L1–L2 in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Neonatal spinal cord ends at L3; adult at L1–L2
options: Lower border of the 1st lumbar vertebra.
Upper border of the 2nd lumbar vertebra.
Upper border of the 3rd lumbar vertebra.

questions.text: A disc prolapsed between T5 and T6 vertebrae would exert pressure upon:
questions.explanation: In the thoracic region, the intervertebral disc is located above the corresponding numbered nerve root because the nerve exits below the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra. Therefore, a disc prolapse between T5 and T6 would compress the T6 nerve root as it exits.
questions.keyConcept: Thoracic disc herniation at T5–T6 compresses the T6 nerve root

questions.text: The nerve(s) that emerge from the vertebral canal above the corresponding vertebrae are:
questions.explanation: The first seven cervical nerves (C1–C7) emerge above their corresponding vertebrae. C8 emerges between C7 and T1. All other spinal nerves emerge below their corresponding vertebrae.
questions.keyConcept: C1–C7 nerves emerge above their corresponding vertebrae

questions.text: The upper 9 thoracic vertebrae contain:
questions.explanation: Due to the cephalad ascent of the spinal cord relative to the vertebral column during development, the upper 9 thoracic vertebrae contain the upper 10 thoracic spinal cord segments. There is approximately a 1–2 segment discrepancy.
questions.keyConcept: Upper 9 thoracic vertebrae house the upper 10 thoracic cord segments
options: Upper 6 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Upper 8 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Upper 10 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Lower 10 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
All thoracic segments of spinal cord.

questions.text: Which of the following is purely sensory?
questions.explanation: The dorsal root of the spinal nerve is purely sensory, containing afferent fibers from the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root is purely motor/efferent. The mixed spinal nerve trunk and its rami contain both sensory and motor fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root = purely sensory

questions.text: How many segments of the spinal cord lie in the vertebral column above the level of lower border of 4th thoracic vertebra (T4)?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord segments above the level of the lower border of the fourth thoracic vertebra include 8 cervical + 4 thoracic = 12 segments.
questions.keyConcept: 12 spinal cord segments lie above T4 vertebral level

questions.text: How many segments of the spinal cord lie in the vertebral column above the level of lower border of 9th thoracic vertebra (T9)?
questions.explanation: Above the lower border of the ninth thoracic vertebra, the spinal cord contains 8 cervical + 9 thoracic = 17 segments. Due to differential growth, the cord segments are higher than their corresponding vertebrae.
questions.keyConcept: 17 spinal cord segments lie above the T9 vertebral level

questions.text: As regards the dorsal root fibers of spinal nerves, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudounipolar (not multipolar). The central processes (axons) of dorsal root ganglion cells enter the spinal cord and may ascend or descend to form long tracts. The peripheral processes (dendrites) connect to receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudounipolar; central processes form ascending tracts
options: Cells of dorsal root ganglion are multipolar.
Central processes (dendrites) of dorsal root fibers are connected to receptors.
Dorsal root fibers give ascending fibers which form long tracts.
Dorsal root fibers give long descending fibers.
After entering spinal cord, dorsal root fibers give long fibers which form intersegmental tracts.

questions.text: As regards the nuclei of the posterior horn of the spinal cord, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The intermediomedial nucleus is associated with the lateral horn and visceral afferent fibers, not the posterior horn. The posteromarginal nucleus is at the tip of the posterior horn. Nucleus proprius lies anterior to substantia gelatinosa.
questions.keyConcept: Intermediomedial nucleus belongs to the lateral horn, not the posterior horn
options: Posteromarginal nucleus - tip of posterior horn.
Nucleus proprius - lies anterior to substantia gelatinosa.
Posterior commissural nuclei - form intersegmental tracts.
Intermediomedial nucleus - serves in transmission of visceral afferent impulses.
Reticular nucleus - lies medial to nucleus proprius.

questions.text: As regards the nuclei of the anterior horn of the spinal cord, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The anteromedial nuclear group extends at all levels of the spinal cord and supplies the axial muscles. Alpha motor neurons supply extrafusal fibers; gamma motor neurons supply intrafusal fibers. The medial group supplies axial muscles, while the lateral group supplies limb muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anteromedial nucleus extends at all cord levels and supplies axial muscles
options: Its alpha neurons supply intrafusal muscle fibers.
Its anteromedial nucleus extends in all levels of spinal cord.
Its medial nuclear group supply muscles of limbs.
Its gamma neurons supply extrafusal muscle fibers.
Its anterolateral nucleus supplies muscles of hands & feet.

questions.text: As regards lamina of spinal cord, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: Lamina IV corresponds to the nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus), not the reticular nucleus. The reticular nucleus corresponds to lamina V. Lamina II = substantia gelatinosa, lamina III = nucleus proprius, lamina VII includes Clarke's nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Lamina IV = nucleus proprius; lamina V = reticular nucleus
options: Lamina II - corresponds to substantia gelatinosa.
Lamina III - corresponds to main sensory nucleus.
Lamina IV - corresponds to reticular nucleus.
Lamina VIII - receives termination of extrapyramidal tracts.

questions.text: The second order neuron in the pathway of pain from the face is:
questions.explanation: Pain from the face travels via the trigeminal nerve. The first order neuron cell bodies are in the trigeminal ganglion, second order neurons are in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of CN V carries face pain 2nd neuron

questions.text: The ability to recognize an unseen familiar object placed in the hand depends on the integrity of which tract?
questions.explanation: Recognizing a familiar object by touch (stereognosis) requires fine touch and proprioception, carried by the cuneate tract from the upper limb. The gracile tract carries these sensations from the lower body.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract carries fine touch from upper limb

questions.text: Gracile tract:
questions.explanation: The gracile tract conveys proprioceptive and fine touch sensations from the lower half of the body. It carries impulses from T7 spinal segment and below, with its fibers passing medially to the cuneate tract.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract carries proprioception from lower body
options: Its sacral fibers are most lateral.
Originates from neurons of lamina I.
Terminates in ventral posterior lateral nucleus of thalamus (VPMN).

questions.text: Cuneate tract:
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract begins at the C8 spinal segment and carries conscious proprioception and fine touch from the upper limb. It does not start at mid-thoracic region—that level marks the beginning of the gracile tract.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract starts at C8, carries upper limb proprioception
options: Its main 2nd neuron is the accessory cuneate nucleus.
Its 3rd neuron passes in the anterior limb of the internal capsule.
Its 3rd neuron terminates in the precentral gyrus.

questions.text: Conscious proprioception from right lower limb are carried by:
questions.explanation: Conscious proprioception from the right lower limb is carried by the right gracile tract, which ascends ipsilaterally in the posterior column and decussates in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract is ipsilateral for lower limb proprioception
options: Tracts of left posterior white column.

questions.text: Unconscious proprioception is carried by:
questions.explanation: Unconscious proprioception, which does not reach conscious awareness, is carried to the cerebellum by the anterior and posterior spinocerebellar tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception

questions.text: The right spinal lemniscus carries sensations of:
questions.explanation: The spinal lemniscus is formed by fibers of the spinothalamic tracts after they decussate. Pain and temperature from the left body crosses to the right spinal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal lemniscus carries contralateral pain/temperature
options: Pain and temperature from left side of the body.
Conscious proprioception from left side of the body.
Muscle tone from right side of body.

questions.text: The cuneate tract carries which of the following sensations?
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract carries fine (discriminative) touch from the upper limb only. Crude touch from upper limb is carried by the ventral spinothalamic tract. Lower limb fine touch uses the gracile tract.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract carries fine touch from upper limb only
options: Crude touch from upper & lower limbs.
Fine touch from upper & lower limbs.
Unconscious proprioception from upper and lower limbs.

questions.text: The left spinal lemniscus carries sensations of:
questions.explanation: The left spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature from the right side of the body (after decussation). Fine touch and proprioception use the medial lemniscus, not the spinal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal lemniscus carries contralateral crude sensation
options: Pain from the left side of the body.
Conscious proprioception from the left side of the body.
Muscle tone from right side of the body.
Crude touch from the right side of the body.
Fine touch from right side of body.

questions.text: The medial most fibers of the gracile tract are:
questions.explanation: The gracile tract carries sensations from the lower body. Sacral fibers are most medial (closest to the midline), while cervical fibers are most lateral in this tract.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers are most medial in gracile tract

questions.text: A lesion in the right gracile tract leads to loss of:
questions.explanation: A lesion in the right gracile tract affects proprioception and fine touch from the right lower limb. Vibration sense testing of the right tibia would be diminished because this tract carries vibration sense.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract lesion affects ipsilateral lower limb vibration
options: Sense of position of left big toe.
Sense of movement of right elbow joint.
Feeling of a pencil put in the right hand.
Site of touch on the right iliac fossa.

questions.text: The first order neuron of pain pathway from face is:
questions.explanation: The first order neuron for pain from the face is the pseudounipolar neuron in the trigeminal ganglion. Its peripheral process receives pain from the face, and central process enters the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal ganglion is 1st neuron for face pain

questions.text: For each structure in the left column, choose the appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: This matching question tests knowledge of sensory pathways. The lateral spinothalamic tract contains the second order neuron for pain from the lower limb, while VPMN is the third order neuron for pain from the face.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral spinothalamic 2nd neuron for body pain

pairs.target: 2nd neuron for pain pathway from lower limb.
2nd neuron for crude touch from thumb.
3rd neuron for pain pathway from eye.
Responsible for head turning in response to pain sensation.

questions.text: For each tract in the left column, choose its descriptive function in the right column:
questions.explanation: This matching tests understanding of ascending tracts. The cuneocerebellar tract begins from the accessory cuneate nucleus and carries unconscious proprioception from cervical segments to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus starts cuneocerebellar tract

pairs.target: Carries unconscious proprioception from cervical segments.
Carries fine touch of big toe.

questions.text: Sacral fibers are the most medial fibers in the spinal cord during its ascend through:
questions.explanation: In the gracile tract, sacral fibers are located most medially (near the posterior median sulcus) while cervical fibers are most lateral. This somatotopic arrangement is maintained throughout the tract.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers most medial in gracile tract

questions.text: Injury of the right cortico-bulbar tract would affect muscles of:
questions.explanation: The corticobulbar tract controls lower facial muscles contralaterally. Lesion of the right corticobulbar tract causes paralysis of the left lower face (contralateral to the lesion).
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar has contralateral control of lower face

questions.text: The corticonuclear tract has unilateral connections with:
questions.explanation: The corticonuclear tract has bilateral connections with most cranial nerve nuclei, except the lower facial nucleus (which is only contralateral) and the trochlear/trigeminal motor nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Lower 7 facial nucleus has unilateral corticonuclear input

questions.text: As regards the motor Decussation, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: Motor decussation (pyramidal decussation) occurs in the caudal part of the medulla, where about 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Motor decussation in caudal medulla
options: It occurs in caudal part of medulla.
It is formed by internal arcuate fibers.
It shows the crossing of 20% of the fibers.
All of the above is true.
None of the above is true.

questions.text: As regards corticobulbar tract, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The corticobulbar tract ends on bilateral cranial nerve nuclei, not only contralateral. Some nuclei (like the lower facial) have predominantly contralateral input, but all have some bilateral contribution.
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar has bilateral cranial nerve connections
options: It ends on contralateral cranial nerve nuclei only.
The part of facial nucleus that controls right half of orbicularis oris muscle receives left corticonuclear tract.
The left genioglossus muscle is controlled by right corticonuclear tract.
It forms a part of upper motor neuron.

questions.text: A patient suffered UMNL paralysis in the left lower limb with loss of vibration sense in the same limb and loss of pain sensation in the right lower limb; the most-likely lesion is:
questions.explanation: Right hemisection (Brown-Sequard): ipsilateral UMNL paralysis, ipsilateral loss of vibration/position sense, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature starting one level below. The description matches right hemisection.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection causes ipsilateral motor/proprioception loss
options: Complete transaction of the spinal cord below TI.
Left hemisection of the spinal cord.
Right hemisection of the spinal cord.

questions.text: For each statement in the left column, choose the appropriate artery in the right column:
questions.explanation: This matching tests blood supply: radicular arteries form the main supply to lumbar segments; anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior horn and lateral horn.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies anterior horn

pairs.premise: 1) Form most blood supply to lumbar segments of spinal cord.
2) Supply lateral horn of spinal cord.
3) May arise from posterior inferior cerebellar artery.
4) Descend in the form of 4 longitudinal arteries.
5) Form the main supply of the cervical part of the spinal cord.

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of posterior horn of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The posterior horn contains four main nuclei: Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) carries pain and temperature; Nucleus proprius (laminae III, IV) carries touch and pressure; Nucleus dorsalis/Clarke's column (lamina VII) is the origin of spinocerebellar tracts; and the Visceral sensory nucleus receives visceral afferents. These nuclei are the second-order neurons in various sensory pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Four nuclei of posterior horn: substantia gelatinosa, nucleus proprius, nucleus dorsalis, visceral sensory nucleus
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of posterior horn: (1) Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) - carries pain and temperature; (2) Nucleus proprius (laminae III, IV) - carries touch and pressure; (3) Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's column, lamina VII) - origin of spinocerebellar tracts; (4) Visceral sensory nucleus - receives visceral afferents.

questions.text: Describe nuclei of lateral horn of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The lateral horn exists at two levels with different functions: T1-L2 contains the intermediolateral nucleus (cell column) for preganglionic sympathetic neurons (sympathetic outflow); S2-S4 contains the sacral parasympathetic nucleus for preganglionic parasympathetic neurons (rest and digest function). The lateral horn is absent at other levels.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral horn: sympathetic (T1-L2 via intermediolateral nucleus) and parasympathetic (S2-S4 via sacral parasympathetic nucleus)
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of lateral horn: (1) Lateral horn is present from C8-L2 (sympathetic outflow) and S2-S4 (parasympathetic outflow). (2) Sympathetic lateral horn nuclei: Intermediolateral nucleus (cell column of T1-L2) - preganglionic sympathetic neurons; (3) Parasympathetic lateral horn nuclei: Sacral parasympathetic nucleus (S2-S4) - preganglionic parasympathetic neurons.

questions.text: Describe corticonuclear (corticobulbar) tract.
questions.explanation: The corticonuclear (corticobulbar) tract: ORIGIN from precentral/postcentral gyri and frontal eye fields; COURSE through posterior limb of internal capsule, basis pedunculi of midbrain, basis pontis, medullary pyramids; TERMINATION on motor nuclei of cranial nerves (III, IV, V, VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XII). Most CN nuclei receive BILATERAL input except the lower facial nucleus (mainly contralateral) and trochlear nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar tract: mostly bilateral cortical input to cranial nerve nuclei (except lower face)
questions.modelAnswer: Corticobulbar (corticomotor) tract: (ORIGIN) Precentral and postcentral gyri, frontal eye fields; (COURSE) Descends through posterior limb of internal capsule, basis pedunculi of midbrain, basis pontis, medullary pyramids; (TERMINATION) On motor nuclei of cranial nerves (CN III, IV, V, VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XII); (CONNECTIONS) Most CN nuclei receive BILATERAL input (except lower facial nucleus - mainly contralateral, and trochlear nucleus).

questions.text: Enumerate the arteries that give radicular arteries to spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Arteries giving radicular arteries to spinal cord include: vertebral arteries, ascending cervical arteries (branch of inferior thyroid artery), deep cervical arteries (branch of costocervical trunk), intercostal arteries (for thoracic segments), lumbar arteries (for lumbar segments), and lateral sacral arteries (for sacral segments). These reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Radicular arteries: vertebral, ascending/deep cervical, intercostal, lumbar, and sacral arteries
questions.modelAnswer: Arteries giving radicular arteries: (1) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES; (2) ASCENDING CERVICAL ARTERIES (branch of inferior thyroid); (3) DEEP CERVICAL ARTERIES (branch of costocervical trunk); (4) INTERCOSTAL ARTERIES (for thoracic segments); (5) LUMBAR ARTERIES (for lumbar segments); (6) LATERAL SACRAL ARTERIES (for sacral segments).

questions.text: Give an account on two main tracts affected by hemisection of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Two main tracts affected by hemisection of spinal cord: (1) LATERAL CORTICOSPINAL TRACT - ipsilateral UMN paralysis below lesion (controls voluntary movement); (2) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACTS - contralateral loss of pain and temperature (after decussation) below lesion. Posterior columns are also affected (ipsilateral loss of proprioception/fine touch).
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection affects: ipsilateral corticospinal (UMN paralysis) and contralateral spinothalamic (pain/temperature loss)
questions.modelAnswer: Two main tracts in hemisection: (1) LATERAL CORTICOSPINAL TRACT - controls voluntary movement; lesion causes ipsilateral UMN paralysis below level of lesion; (2) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACTS - carry pain and temperature; lesion causes contralateral loss of pain/temperature (after decussation) below lesion. Other tracts affected: posterior columns (ipsilateral loss of proprioception/fine touch).

questions.text: Describe the effect of complete transection of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Complete transection of spinal cord: IMMEDIATE (spinal shock): flaccid paralysis, loss of all sensations, absent reflexes below lesion. AFTER WEEKS: spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski. SENSORY: complete loss below lesion. AUTONOMIC: loss of bladder/bowel control, sexual dysfunction. All functions lost at and below the level of lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Complete transection: initial spinal shock (flaccid) → later spastic paralysis, total sensory and autonomic loss below lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Complete transection of spinal cord: (IMMEDIATE) Spinal shock - flaccid paralysis, loss of all sensations, absent reflexes below lesion; (AFTER WEEKS) Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski; (SENSORY) Loss of pain, temperature, touch, proprioception below lesion; (AUTONOMIC) Loss of bladder/bowel control, sexual dysfunction; (LEVEL) All functions lost at and below the lesion.

questions.text: Lesion of which cerebral area in left hemisphere causes motor aphasia?
questions.explanation: Motor aphasia (Broca's aphasia) results from lesion of Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus, which is responsible for speech production. In the dominant hemisphere, this is typically the left side.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area in inferior frontal gyrus causes motor aphasia

questions.text: Motor aphasia is due to lesion of the following area:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus and is responsible for motor (expressive) speech. Lesions cause non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area - motor/expressive speech area

questions.text: Changes in personality and judgment occur in lesion of:
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex (anterior to the precentral gyrus) is responsible for personality, judgment, executive function, and social behavior. Lesions cause changes in personality and impaired judgment.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal area controls personality and judgment

questions.text: Injury to the left paracentral lobule leads to paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The paracentral lobule is the continuation of the primary motor and sensory areas onto the medial surface of the hemisphere. The left paracentral lobule controls the right lower limb (leg and foot) via the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Left paracentral lobule controls right leg

questions.text: Injury to the right paracentral lobule leads to paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The right paracentral lobule controls the left leg. Since motor pathways cross (decussate), injury to the right paracentral lobule causes paralysis of the contralateral (left) lower limb.
questions.keyConcept: Right paracentral lobule controls left leg

questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Prefrontal area.
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex is responsible for personality, social behavior, and executive functions. Lesions here commonly result in personality changes, including disinhibition and apathy.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal area lesion causes personality changes

questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Frontal eye field.
questions.explanation: The frontal eye field (area 8) controls voluntary conjugate eye movements. Lesions cause inability to look toward the opposite side (loss of conjugate eye deviation).
questions.keyConcept: Frontal eye field controls voluntary eye movement

questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Superior parietal lobule.
questions.explanation: The superior parietal lobule is involved in spatial awareness and stereognosis (ability to recognize objects by touch). Lesions cause astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and hemispatial neglect.
questions.keyConcept: Superior parietal lobule mediates stereognosis

questions.text: Hind brain (Rhombencephalon) includes all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes the medulla oblongata, pons, and cerebellum. The crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (not hindbrain), containing corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Crus cerebri is midbrain, not hindbrain

questions.text: One of the following is not a content of the interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is a space between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents include the oculomotor nerve, mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum, posterior perforated substance, and cerebral peduncles. The anterior perforated substance is lateral to the optic tract, not in the interpeduncular fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior perforated substance not in interpeduncular fossa

questions.text: A nerve attached to the cerebello-pontine angle:
questions.explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) is attached at the cerebellopontine angle, along with the facial nerve. This is the angle between the pons, cerebellum, and olive where these nerves emerge.
questions.keyConcept: CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle

questions.text: Which of the following structures lies between limbs of inferior fovea?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus is a bump in the floor of the fourth ventricle formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve wrapping around it. It lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus between limbs of inferior fovea

questions.text: Facial colliculus overlies:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus overlies the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers that loop around it (the facial nerve genu). This creates a prominence in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus overlies abducent nucleus

questions.text: The facial colliculus is formed by:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus is formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve (motor root) that curve around it internally. These fibers form the facial nerve genu in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus formed by CN VI nucleus and CN VII fibers
options: Abducent nucleus and facial nerve fibers.
Facial motor nucleus and abducent nerve fibers.

questions.text: Posterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa is formed by:
questions.explanation: The posterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa is formed by the cerebral peduncles. These are two large bundles of descending fibers on either side of the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncles form posterolateral boundary

questions.text: All the following structures wind around cerebral peduncles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is an outpouching of the brain and does not wind around the cerebral peduncles; it runs in the optic tract to the lateral geniculate body. The trochlear nerve wraps around the cerebral peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve does not wind around cerebral peduncle

questions.text: All the following form boundaries of interpeduncular fossa EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is not a boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. The boundaries are: cerebral peduncles (posterolateral), upper border of pons (inferior), optic chiasma (superior), and optic tract (posterolateral).
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve not boundary of interpeduncular fossa

questions.text: Contents of interpeduncular fossa belong to:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is located in the midbrain, between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents (oculomotor nerve, posterior perforated substance, etc.) are all midbrain structures.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa belongs to midbrain

questions.text: The fibers present in the medial 1/5 of the crus cerebri are:
questions.explanation: The frontal pontine fibers (from prefrontal cortex) occupy the medial one-fifth of the crus cerebri. Corticospinal fibers are in the middle three-fifths, and parieto/temporopontine fibers are in the lateral one-fifth.
questions.keyConcept: Frontopontine fibers in medial 1/5 of crus cerebri

questions.text: Which of the following olivary nuclear complex is not contained in medulla?
questions.explanation: The medial accessory olive is part of the olivary nuclear complex within the medulla. The superior olivary nucleus is in the pons, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Superior olivary nucleus not in medulla

questions.text: The fibers in the lateral 1/5 of crus cerebri include:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus connects the vestibular nuclei with the nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI to coordinate eye movements. It also connects with the spinal cord for head and neck reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with III, IV, VI nuclei

questions.text: For each nucleus in left column, choose its appropriate description in right column:
questions.explanation: The muscles NOT supplied by nucleus ambiguus include the tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini, which are branchiomotor muscles of the trigeminal nerve (motor V).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus does not supply tensor muscles

pairs.target: e. Its fibers end in VPMN of thalamus.
d. A convoluted mass of gray matter.
a. Carries unconscious proprioception from upper limbs & neck
b. Affect level of arousal & consciousness.
c. It gives anterior external arcuate fibers.

questions.text: Basis pontis contains all the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve receives proprioceptive afferents from muscles of mastication and extraocular muscles. It is unique as a nucleus containing primary sensory neuron cell bodies (neural crest derived).
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus receives mastication proprioception

questions.text: As regards auditory pathway, for each description in left column, choose its appropriate part from right column:
questions.explanation: This matching tests cranial nerve nuclei: hypoglossal nucleus ( GSE) - tongue muscles; nucleus ambiguus (SVE) - pharynx/larynx; dorsal motor nucleus of X (GVE) - thoracic/abdominal viscera.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nucleus supplies tongue muscles

pairs.premise: 57) Some of its fibers end in inferior colliculus.
60) Originates from bipolar nerve cells in spiral ganglion.

questions.text: As regards the medial longitudinal bundle, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus runs in the brainstem and receives input from the vestibular nuclei, interstitial nucleus of Cajal, and the superior colliculus. It coordinates head and eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with eye movement nuclei
options: It extends from thalamus to spinal cord.
In spinal cord, it is formed of ascending & descending tracts.
Its ascending fibers project to motor nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV & V.
Its descending fibers include tectospinal fibers.
Its ascending fibers are connected with interstitial nucleus of Cajal.

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei represents the visceral afferent column (GVA & SVA)?
questions.explanation: Special visceral afferent nuclei receive taste sensation. The nucleus solitarius (particularly its gustatory part) receives taste fibers from CN VII, IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Special visceral afferent - taste fibers

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei represents the visceral afferent column?
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini muscles are supplied by the trigeminal nerve (V3), not by nucleus ambiguus. All other pharyngeal arch muscles are supplied by nucleus ambiguus.
questions.keyConcept: Tensor muscles supplied by CN V, not nucleus ambiguus

questions.text: The nucleus ambiguus does not supply the following muscle(s):
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nucleus is the only somatic efferent nucleus in the brainstem that supplies muscles of somite origin. Other somatic efferent nuclei (III, IV, VI) are in the midbrain/pons.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nucleus is SE column in medulla

questions.text: Choose the nucleus from the right column that suits the statement in the left column:
questions.explanation: The facial nerve nuclei include: facial motor nucleus (SVE), superior salivary nucleus (GVE - parasympathetic), nucleus solitarius (SVA - taste), and mesencephalic nucleus of V (for facial proprioception).
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve has motor, parasympathetic, and taste nuclei

pairs.target: e. Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus.

questions.text: Somatic efferent column of nuclei includes:
questions.explanation: The nucleus that receives taste fibers is the nucleus solitarius (solitary nucleus), particularly its rostral/gustatory part. It receives SVA fibers from CN VII (via chorda tympani), IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius receives taste sensation

questions.text: General visceral efferent column includes the following nuclei Except:
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus supplies muscles of the larynx. However, all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of X).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus supplies laryngeal muscles via X

questions.text: Special visceral afferent nuclei include:
questions.explanation: This is an INCORRECT question about medial longitudinal bundle connections. The MLF does connect the vestibular nuclei with cranial nerve nuclei III, IV, and VI to coordinate eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with eye movement nuclei

questions.text: Special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) column includes:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the only pontine cranial nerve attached at the junction of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle, supplying the second pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch) muscles.
questions.keyConcept: CN V attached at pons-middle cerebellar peduncle junction

questions.text: Nucleus ambiguuus supplies all the following muscles EXCPT:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is the first-order neuron for proprioception from muscles of mastication. Unique among sensory nuclei, it contains cell bodies of primary afferent neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus of V is 1st neuron for mastication proprioception

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei represents the somatic efferent column?
questions.explanation: This matching tests nuclei: facial nucleus - facial muscles; nucleus ambiguus - pharyngeal muscles; dorsal motor nucleus of X - visceral organs. All are branchiomotor or visceral motor nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nucleus supplies muscles of facial expression

questions.text: The special visceral efferent column of nuclei:
questions.explanation: This matching tests nucleus functions: hypoglossal - tongue movement; nucleus ambiguus - swallowing/phonation; dorsal motor X - parasympathetic to viscera; vestibular - balance; cochlear - hearing.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus involved in swallowing and speech
options: Supplies muscles derived from pharyngeal arches.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) includes: ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss (spinal V), contralateral body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic), dysphagia, hoarseness, ataxia, vertigo, nystagmus, Horner syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome includes vestibular symptoms
questions.modelAnswer: This question asks to identify the INCORRECT statement about cranial nerve nuclei. The nucleus solitarius is the visceral afferent column, NOT the GVE column. GVE (parasympathetic) nuclei include: Edinger-Westphal (III), superior salivary (VII), inferior salivary (IX), dorsal motor nucleus of X.

questions.text: For each nucleus in left column, choose the appropriate structure supplied by it in right column:
questions.explanation: Different cranial nerve nuclei supply specific structures. The facial nucleus supplies muscles of facial expression. Nucleus ambiguus supplies pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles. Dorsal motor nucleus of X supplies thoracic/abdominal viscera. Hypoglossal nucleus supplies tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial nerve nuclei have specific structural targets

questions.text: For each nucleus in left column, choose the appropriate function in right column:
questions.explanation: Different nuclei serve specific functions: hypoglossal for tongue, nucleus ambiguus for swallowing/phonation, dorsal motor X for parasympathetic regulation, vestibular for balance, and cochlear for hearing.
questions.keyConcept: Each cranial nerve nucleus serves specific function

questions.text: Describe boundaries & contents of interpeduncular fossa.
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is bounded: ANTERIORLY by the optic chiasma; LATERALLY by the cerebral peduncles; POSTERIORLY by the mammillary bodies; INFERIORLY by the pons. CONTENTS: (1) Posterior perforated substance (contains central artery of midbrain); (2) Basilar artery bifurcation; (3) Mamillary bodies form the posterior boundary. It is a clinically important space for aneurysms and tumors.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa: bounded by optic chiasma anteriorly, cerebral peduncles laterally, mammillary bodies posteriorly
questions.modelAnswer: SENSORY DECUSSATION: (LOCATION) Caudal medulla; (PROCESS) Second-order neurons from gracile and cuneate nuclei send fibers that become internal arcuate fibers and cross in the medulla; (RESULT) Forms the medial lemniscus which ascends to the contralateral thalamus; (IMPORTANCE) Explains why dorsal column lesions cause ipsilateral sensory loss.

questions.text: Give an account on different lemnisci (beginning, termination & function).
questions.explanation: There are four major lemnisci in the brainstem: (1) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS - from dorsal column nuclei (gracile/cuneate) through medulla, pons, midbrain to VPL thalamus; carries conscious proprioception and fine touch; (2) SPINAL LEMNISCUS - from spinothalamic tracts to VPL; carries pain and temperature; (3) TRIGEMINAL LEMNISCUS - from trigeminal sensory nuclei to VPM; carries face sensation; (4) LATERAL LEMNISCUS - from cochlear nuclei to inferior colliculus; carries auditory information.
questions.keyConcept: Four lemnisci: medial (proprioception/touch), spinal (pain/temperature), trigeminal (face sensation), lateral (hearing)
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF VAGUS NERVE: (1) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to thoracic and abdominal viscera; (2) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (SVE) - motor to pharynx and larynx (via pharyngeal branch and recurrent laryngeal nerve); (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA/GVA) - taste from epiglottis and general visceral sensation; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (GSA) - sensory from larynx.

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of glossopharyngeal N. & structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: Nuclei of the glossopharyngeal nerve: (1) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (SVE) - motor to stylopharyngeus muscle (elevates pharynx); (2) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to parotid gland via otic ganglion; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA/GVA) - taste from posterior one-third of tongue and visceral sensation; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (GSA) - general sensation from middle ear, pharynx, and posterior tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nuclei: nucleus ambiguus (stylopharyngeus), inferior salivary (parotid), nucleus solitarius (taste), spinal V (sensation)
questions.modelAnswer: (Location) Cerebellopontine angle tumor - affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) causing hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus; CN VII (facial) causing facial paralysis; later cerebellum causing ataxia; CN V causing facial sensory loss; (Other features) Nystagmus, vomiting, headache.

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of SVE column & the structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: The inferior hypophyseal (pituitary) artery branches from the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery. The superior hypophyseal arteries come from the supraclinoid part.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior hypophyseal artery from cavernous ICA
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF SVE COLUMN: (1) TRIGEMINAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (V) in pons → muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini; (2) FACIAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (VII) in pons → muscles of facial expression, stapedius; (3) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (IX, X, XI) in medulla → stylopharyngeus, pharynx/larynx muscles, sternocleidomastoid, trapezius; (4) ACCESSORY NUCLEUS (spinal part of XI).

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of GSA column & the structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (specifically the ophthalmic division V1) provides sensory innervation to the dura above the tentorium cerebelli. The trochlear nerve also contributes.
questions.keyConcept: CN V1 innervates dura above tentorium
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GSA COLUMN: (1) TRIGEMINAL NUCLEI (principal and spinal) in pons/medulla → general sensation from face, scalp, teeth, meninges; (2) COCHLEAR NUCLEI (dorsal and ventral) at pontomedullary junction → hearing; (3) VESTIBULAR NUCLEI (superior, medial, lateral, inferior) → balance and spatial orientation. These nuclei receive afferents from head and neck receptors.

questions.text: Cranial dura is supplied by all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The cranial dura mater receives sensory innervation from the maxillary and mandibular divisions of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), as well as from upper cervical spinal nerves (C1-C3) via the hypoglossal, vagus, and glossopharyngeal nerves (for the posterior cranial fossa). The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) does NOT supply the cranial dura; its sensory fibers are distributed to the pharynx, middle ear, carotid sinus, and posterior tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) does NOT innervate the cranial dura.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered as a multiple venous sinus?
questions.explanation: The basilar plexus of sinuses is an irregular, intercommunicating venous plexus located on the dorsum sellae and basi-occiput, posterior to the cavernous sinuses. It connects the two inferior petrosal sinuses and communicates with the vertebral venous plexus and internal vertebral venous plexus, forming an important alternative venous drainage pathway from the cranial cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar plexus of sinuses is a multiple/intercommunicating venous plexus posterior to cavernous sinuses.

questions.text: As regards trigeminal ganglion, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian ganglion) is a crescent-shaped sensory ganglion located in Meckel's cave, which lies on the anterior surface of the petrous temporal bone, NOT at its apex. It gives rise to the ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular divisions anterolaterally. Its central processes form the sensory root that enters the pons, while its peripheral processes form the three divisions.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal ganglion lies in Meckel's cave on the anterior surface of petrous temporal bone, not at the apex.
options: Anterolaterally, it gives attachment to divisions of trigeminal nerve.
It lies at apex of petreous temporal bone.
Central processes of its cells form sensory root of trigeminal nerve.

questions.text: Enumerate venous sinuses enclosed within Falx cerebri, Falx cerebelli & Tentorium cerebelli.
questions.explanation: Venous sinuses are enclosed within dural folds at specific anatomical locations. The falx cerebri contains the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses. The falx cerebelli contains the occipital sinus. The tentorium cerebelli contains the transverse, superior petrosal, and straight sinuses within its margins.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri: superior/inferior sagittal; Falx cerebelli: occipital; Tentorium: transverse, superior petrosal, straight.
questions.modelAnswer: Sinuses within the falx cerebri: superior sagittal sinus (superior attached margin) and inferior sagittal sinus (free lower margin). Sinuses within the falx cerebelli: occipital sinus. Sinuses within the tentorium cerebelli: transverse sinus (posterior attached margin), superior petrosal sinus (anterior attached margin), and straight sinus (at the junction of falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli).

questions.text: Describe surface anatomy of middle meningeal artery.
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery is the largest meningeal artery supplying the dura and skull bones. Surgical knowledge of its surface anatomy is essential for trephination and preventing injury during temporal surgery.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery enters through foramen spinosum; anterior branch runs toward pterion; posterior branch runs posterolaterally.
questions.modelAnswer: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery in the infratemporal fossa that enters the skull through the foramen spinosum. Its anterior branch runs upward and forward toward the pterion, grooving the parietal bone deeply. Its posterior branch runs backward and upward toward the lambdoid suture. Its surface marking on the lateral skull can be traced from the posterior aspect of the zygomatic bone, upward and slightly backward toward the parietal eminence.

questions.text: The nerve that emerges between the two heads of lateral pterygoid is:
questions.explanation: The buccal nerve is a sensory branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It emerges between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle and supplies the skin of the cheek, buccal mucosa, and skin over the buccinator muscle. The inferior alveolar nerve descends deep to both heads, the masseteric nerve passes above the upper head, the lingual nerve descends between the medial pterygoid and mandible, and the auriculotemporal nerve emerges behind the temporomandibular joint.
questions.keyConcept: Buccal nerve emerges between the two heads of lateral pterygoid muscle.

questions.text: The structure attached to the pterygoid hamulus is the:
questions.explanation: The pterygomandibular raphe is a tendinous band attached superiorly to the pterygoid hamulus of the medial pterygoid plate and inferiorly to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It represents the junction between the superior pharyngeal constrictor posteriorly and the buccinator anteriorly, serving as an important anatomical landmark during inferior alveolar nerve block anesthesia.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygomandibular raphe is attached to the pterygoid hamulus.

questions.text: The parasympathetic root to submandibular ganglion is derived from:
questions.explanation: The submandibular ganglion receives its parasympathetic preganglionic fibers from the superior salivatory nucleus via the nervus intermedius, greater petrosal nerve, and facial nerve. These fibers continue in the chorda tympani nerve (branch of CN VII), which joins the lingual nerve and synapses in the submandibular ganglion. Postganglionic fibers then innervate the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. The lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX) supplies the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic root to submandibular ganglion is derived from the chorda tympani nerve (CN VII).

questions.text: Enumerate boundaries of Infratemporal fossa.
