questions.explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) corresponds to Rexed lamina II of the posterior horn, specializing in pain and temperature modulation.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia gelatinosa lamina

questions.text: Clark’s nucleus (dorsal nucleus) is located in which lamina?
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is located in Rexed lamina VII at T1-L2 levels, serving as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus lamina

questions.text: A patient with a spinal cord lesion has loss of vibration and position sense in both legs but normal pain and temperature sensation. Which tract is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Bilateral loss of vibration and position sense with preserved pain/temperature indicates gracile tract lesion, as it carries proprioception and vibration from the legs.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract lesion

questions.text: Operant conditioning is a type of:
questions.explanation: Operant (instrumental) conditioning is associative learning where behavior is modified by its consequences (reward or punishment).
questions.keyConcept: Operant conditioning

questions.text: Semantic memory refers to:
questions.explanation: Semantic memory stores general facts, concepts, and knowledge independent of personal experience (declarative/explicit memory).
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory
options: Memory of facts and general knowledge

questions.text: The representational (non‑dominant) hemisphere in most people is described by which feature?
questions.explanation: The representational (non-dominant) hemisphere in most people lies in the right hemisphere and is specialized for spatial and holistic processing.
questions.keyConcept: Non-dominant hemisphere
options: It is responsible for language comprehension.
It always lies in the left hemisphere.
It is concerned with analytical tasks.

questions.text: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that increases the permeability of the postsynaptic membrane to which ion?
questions.explanation: GABA-A receptors are ligand-gated chloride channels; chloride influx hyperpolarizes the neuron, causing inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: GABA mechanism

questions.text: Fast pain (first pain) is transmitted to the CNS by which fibres?
questions.explanation: A-delta fibers (myelinated, fast-conducting) transmit first/quick pain, while C fibers (unmyelinated) transmit slow, throbbing second pain.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain fibers

questions.text: Which of the following inhibits pain sensation?
questions.explanation: Opioid receptor stimulation activates descending pain inhibition pathways, reducing pain transmission at the spinal cord level.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid pain inhibition
options: Activation of the lateral spinothalamic tract

questions.text: The mood stabiliser with delayed onset, narrow therapeutic index, and requirement for blood level monitoring is:
questions.explanation: Lithium has delayed onset (weeks), narrow therapeutic index (0.6-1.2 mEq/L), and requires regular serum level monitoring.
questions.keyConcept: Lithium characteristics

questions.text: Which combination of drugs should be avoided because both can cause agranulocytosis?
questions.explanation: Clozapine and carbamazepine both cause agranulocytosis; their combination dramatically increases this risk and is contraindicated.
questions.keyConcept: Agranulocytosis drug interaction

questions.text: The only medically justified long‑term use of phenobarbital is for:
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital is justified long-term only for certain epilepsies (generalized tonic-clonic, partial seizures) due to its side effect profile.
questions.keyConcept: Phenobarbital use

questions.text: The main benefit of adding carbidopa to levodopa in Sinemet is that carbidopa:
questions.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, preventing peripheral levodopa conversion and increasing CNS availability.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa mechanism
options: Inhibits peripheral aromatic L‑amino acid decarboxylase

questions.text: The potency of inhaled anaesthetics is quantitatively defined as the:
questions.explanation: MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) defines potency as the alveolar concentration that prevents movement in 50% of patients to a surgical stimulus.
questions.keyConcept: Inhalational anesthetic MAC

questions.text: An important virulence factor of *Cryptococcus neoformans* is the production of:
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans produces melanin via phenol oxidase, which protects against oxidative stress and is a major virulence factor.
questions.keyConcept: Cryptococcus virulence

questions.text: The vaccine used for protection against tetanus consists of:
questions.explanation: Tetanus vaccine contains inactivated tetanus toxin (toxoid) that stimulates antibody production without causing disease.
questions.keyConcept: Tetanus vaccine

questions.text: Which characteristic is true of *Listeria monocytogenes*?
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a psychrophile that can grow at refrigerator temperatures (4°C), enabling it to contaminate refrigerated foods.
questions.keyConcept: Listeria cold tolerance
options: It is strictly a human pathogen.
It can grow at refrigerator temperature (4°C).

questions.text: Which enzyme is stimulated by cortisol to increase epinephrine synthesis?
questions.explanation: PNMT (phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase) converts norepinephrine to epinephrine and is induced by cortisol in the adrenal medulla.
questions.keyConcept: PNMT epinephrine synthesis

questions.text: Which cofactor is required for the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine?
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as cofactor to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine; BH4 deficiency causes PKU.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylation

questions.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is a coenzyme for the oxidative decarboxylation of:
questions.explanation: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) is the coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids including pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and branched-chain ketoacids.
questions.keyConcept: TPP coenzyme function

questions.text: Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, death) is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Pellagra results from niacin (B3) deficiency, classically presenting with the 4 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death if untreated.
questions.keyConcept: Pellagra deficiency

questions.text: Methyl‑THF donates its methyl group to homocysteine to form:
questions.explanation: Methyl-THF transfers its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.
questions.keyConcept: Methyl-THF function

questions.text: Glutamate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by:
questions.explanation: ADP and GDP are allosteric activators of glutamate dehydrogenase, which catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate dehydrogenase regulation

questions.text: Serotonin is synthesised from which amino acid?
questions.explanation: Serotonin (5-HT) is synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase (rate-limiting) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesis precursor

questions.text: Mention the 2 enlargements present in the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The spinal cord has cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L2-S3) enlargements for limb innervation, corresponding to brachial and lumbosacral plexuses.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord enlargements
questions.modelAnswer: Cervical enlargement and lumbar enlargement.

questions.text: Compare between the spinal cord of the adult and the newborn:
questions.explanation: In adults the spinal cord extends from C1 to L1 vertebra, while in newborns it extends from C1 to L3 vertebra due to differential vertebral column growth.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord extent
questions.modelAnswer: Adult: C1 till L1; Newborn: C1 till L3.

questions.text: Extent of the scalp:
questions.explanation: The scalp extends from the supraorbital margin anteriorly to the external occipital protuberance posteriorly, and to the superior temporal line laterally.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp extent
questions.modelAnswer: Anteriorly: supraorbital margin; Posteriorly: external occipital protuberance and highest nuchal line; Laterally: superior temporal line.

questions.text: Effects of dense connective tissue in scalp:
questions.explanation: Dense connective tissue in the scalp means infections remain localized, wounds gape less due to fibrous septa, and small wounds cause profuse bleeding from arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp dense connective tissue
questions.modelAnswer: Infection remains localized, wounds don't gap, small wound causes profuse bleeding.

questions.text: Compare frontal and occipital belly nerve supply:
questions.explanation: The frontal belly of occipitofrontalis is innervated by the temporal branch of facial nerve; the occipital belly is innervated by the posterior auricular branch.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis innervation
questions.modelAnswer: Frontal belly: temporal branch of facial nerve; Occipital belly: posterior auricular branch of facial nerve.

questions.text: Why is loose connective tissue the dangerous layer?
questions.explanation: The loose areolar tissue (dangerous layer) contains valveless emissary veins connecting scalp veins to intracranial venous sinuses, allowing infection spread.
questions.keyConcept: Dangerous layer of scalp
questions.modelAnswer: Because its emissary veins can spread infection from scalp to cranial cavity.

questions.text: Sensory nerve supply of scalp:
questions.explanation: Anterior to auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal nerves; posterior to auricle: great auricular, lesser/greater occipital, third occipital.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp sensory innervation
questions.modelAnswer: In front of auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal; Behind auricle: great auricular, lesser occipital, greater occipital, third occipital.

questions.text: Boundaries of face:
questions.explanation: The face is bounded superiorly by the hairline, inferiorly by the lower mandibular border, and laterally by the auricles connecting both sides.
questions.keyConcept: Facial boundaries
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: hair line; Inferior: lower border of mandible; Sideways: from one auricle to the other.

questions.text: Facial artery terminates by anastomosing with:
questions.explanation: The facial artery terminates by anastomosing with the dorsal nasal artery, completing the arterial supply around the eye and nose.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery termination
questions.modelAnswer: The facial artery terminates by anastomosing with the dorsal nasal artery (a branch of the ophthalmic artery), forming rich collateral anastomoses at the angle of the mouth and near the nose. It also anastomoses with the transverse facial artery and the labial arteries.

questions.text: 2 branches of facial artery in face:
questions.explanation: The two terminal branches of the facial artery within the face are the superior labial artery and inferior labial artery supplying the lips.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery face branches
questions.modelAnswer: Superior labial and Inferior labial.

questions.text: Branches of ophthalmic nerve in face:
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches in the face include supratrochlear, supraorbital (from frontal nerve), and infratrochlear nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Ophthalmic nerve facial branches
questions.modelAnswer: Supratrochlear, supraorbital, palpebral branch of lacrimal, infratrochlear.

questions.text: 3 branches of maxillary nerve:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off infraorbital, zygomatic, and greater palatine nerves in the face, supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper teeth.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve branches
questions.modelAnswer: Infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, greater palatine nerve.

questions.text: 3 branches of infraorbital nerve:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (terminal branch of V2) gives inferior palpebral, external nasal, superior labial, and anterior superior alveolar branches.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve branches
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior palpebral, external nasal, superior labial, anterior superior alveolar.

questions.text: Branches of mandibular nerve in face:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) gives mental and auriculotemporal branches on the face; the motor branches (masseteric, temporal, buccal) supply muscles of mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve facial branches
questions.modelAnswer: Mental nerve (from inferior alveolar), auriculotemporal nerve.

questions.text: Muscles of facial expression develop from:
questions.explanation: Muscles of facial expression develop from the second pharyngeal arch (hyoid arch), innervated by CN VII (facial nerve).
questions.keyConcept: Facial muscle embryology
questions.modelAnswer: Second pharyngeal arch mesoderm.

questions.text: Lesion of areas 5 & 7 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of areas 5 and 7 (superior parietal lobule) causes sensory neglect of contralateral side, astereognosis, and optic ataxia.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 5-7 lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Sensory neglect, astereognosis, and optic ataxia.

questions.text: Site of inferior parietal lobule:
questions.explanation: The inferior parietal lobule (areas 40, 39) is located below the intraparietal sulcus, behind the lateral sulcus, comprising supramarginal and angular gyri.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule
questions.modelAnswer: Below intraparietal sulcus, consisting of angular and supramarginal gyri.

questions.text: Lesion of inferior parietal lobule causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of the inferior parietal lobule causes Gerstmann syndrome (left lesion): agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.

questions.text: Body representation of premotor area:
questions.explanation: The premotor area (area 6) has a somatotopic representation similar to M1, controlling proximal and trunk muscles with less discrete localization.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor body map
questions.modelAnswer: Similar to motor cortex but controls proximal muscles.

questions.text: Lesion of area 6 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of area 6 (premotor area) causes loss of skilled movement, motor apraxia, and rigidity without true paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Area 6 lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Motor apraxia, loss of skilled movement, rigidity.

questions.text: Site of frontal eye field:
questions.explanation: The frontal eye field (area 8) is located in the middle frontal gyrus anterior to the premotor area, controlling voluntary eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal eye field location
questions.modelAnswer: Middle frontal gyrus, anterior to premotor area.

questions.text: Lesion of area 8 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of area 8 (frontal eye field) causes conjugate deviation of eyes toward the side of the lesion (inability to look away).
questions.keyConcept: Area 8 lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Conjugate eye deviation toward the lesion.

questions.text: Lesion of SMA causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of SMA causes loss of spontaneous movement, speech initiation, and bilateral motor planning without paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: SMA lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Loss of spontaneous movement and speech initiation.

questions.text: 3 neurons for pain and temperature from body:
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature from the body uses three neurons: DRG (pseudounipolar), substantia gelatinosa (second order), VPL thalamus (third order).
questions.keyConcept: Pain temperature body pathway
questions.modelAnswer: First order: dorsal root ganglion; Second order: substantia gelatinosa; Third order: VPL thalamus.

questions.text: 3 neurons for pain and temperature from face:
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature from face: first order in trigeminal ganglion, second order in spinal trigeminal nucleus, third order in VPM thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Pain temperature face pathway
questions.modelAnswer: First order: trigeminal ganglion; Second order: spinal trigeminal nucleus; Third order: VPM thalamus.

questions.text: 3 neurons for conscious proprioception and fine touch:
questions.explanation: Conscious proprioception uses three neurons: DRG (first order), gracile/cuneate nuclei (second order, crossing in medulla), VPL thalamus (third order), via medial lemniscus to cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Conscious proprioception pathway
questions.modelAnswer: First order: DRG; Second order: gracile/cuneate nuclei; Third order: VPL thalamus.

questions.text: Tracts carrying unconscious proprioception from lower limb:
questions.explanation: Unconscious proprioception from the lower limb is carried by the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus) to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Lower limb proprioception tracts
questions.modelAnswer: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract and ventral spinocerebellar tract.

questions.text: Origin of olivospinal tract:
questions.explanation: The olivospinal tract arises from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla and descends to the spinal cord to influence motor activity.
questions.keyConcept: Olivospinal tract origin
questions.modelAnswer: The olivospinal tract (olivary tract) originates from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla oblongata. These fibers descend in the spinal cord within the lateral funiculus and terminate on interneurons in the intermediate gray matter, primarily at cervical levels.

questions.text: 3 arteries supplying spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The three arteries supplying the spinal cord are the anterior spinal artery (ventral median spinal artery) and two posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord blood supply
questions.modelAnswer: One anterior spinal artery and two posterior spinal arteries.

questions.text: Artery supplying medial medulla and anterior 2/3 of spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla and anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the corticospinal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery
questions.modelAnswer: The anterior spinal artery (ASA) supplies the medial medulla and the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. It arises from the vertebral arteries and descends through the anterior median fissure, supplying the pyramids, medial lemnisci, and corticospinal tracts.

questions.text: Origin of radicular arteries:
questions.explanation: Radicular arteries arise segmentally from various aortic branches including vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, and first lumbar arteries, following nerve roots to supply the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Radicular arteries have segmental origins from aortic branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, 1st lumbar.

questions.text: 6 veins draining spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The spinal cord venous drainage follows a symmetrical pattern with anteromedian and posteromedian veins running vertically, plus four additional veins accompanying the ventral and dorsal nerve roots.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord has six longitudinal veins: anteromedian, posteromedian, and four radicular veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteromedian, posteromedian, four veins along ventral and dorsal roots.

questions.text: Hemisection:
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection) causes ipsilateral motor loss and all sensory loss at the lesion level, ipsilateral proprioceptive loss below the lesion, and contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection causes ipsilateral motor and contralateral pain loss below lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: At lesion: ipsilateral loss of all sensations, ipsilateral LMNL; Below lesion ipsilateral: loss of proprioception, UMNL; Below lesion contralateral: loss of pain and temperature.

questions.text: 3 lobes (functional):
questions.explanation: The cerebellum's functional lobes include archicerebellum (vestibular coordination), paleocerebellum (postural control), and neocerebellum (skilled movements).
questions.keyConcept: Three functional cerebellar lobes: archi-, paleo-, and neocerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: Archicerebellum, paleocerebellum, neocerebellum.

questions.text: Efferent fibers of ICP:
questions.explanation: Efferent fibers of the inferior cerebellar peduncle include cerebellovestibular fibers (to vestibular nuclei), cerebelloreticular fibers (to reticular formation), and cerebello-olivary fibers (to inferior olive).
questions.keyConcept: ICP efferents: cerebellovestibular, cerebelloreticular, cerebello-olivary.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebellovestibular, cerebelloreticular, cerebello‑olivary.

questions.text: Nerves affected by cerebellopontine angle tumor:
questions.explanation: A cerebellopontine angle tumor (typically acoustic neuroma) first affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) causing hearing loss and vertigo, then CN VII (facial) causing facial weakness.
questions.keyConcept: CPA tumor affects cranial nerves 7 and 8.
questions.modelAnswer: A cerebellopontine angle tumor (commonly vestibular schwannoma / acoustic neuroma) affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) causing hearing loss and tinnitus; CN V (trigeminal nerve) causing facial numbness; and CN VII (facial nerve) causing facial palsy. Brainstem compression may also occur.

questions.text: 4 structures winding around cerebral peduncle:
questions.explanation: Four structures wind around the cerebral peduncle: optic tract (medial), trochlear nerve (lateral), posterior cerebral artery (superior), and basal vein (dorsal).
questions.keyConcept: Structures around cerebral peduncle: optic tract, trochlear nerve, PCA, basal vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Optic tract, Trochlear nerve, Posterior cerebral artery, Basal vein.

questions.text: Boundaries of interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is bounded anteriorly by the optic chiasma, anterolaterally by the optic tract, posterolaterally by the cerebral peduncle, and posteriorly by the upper pons.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa boundaries: optic chiasma, optic tract, cerebral peduncle, upper pons.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: optic chiasma; Anterolateral: optic tract; Posterolateral: cerebral peduncle; Posterior: upper border of pons.

questions.text: Contents of interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa contains the tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance (allowing blood vessels to penetrate), and the oculomotor nerve emerging between the cerebral peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Fossa contents: tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, perforated substance, oculomotor nerve.
questions.modelAnswer: Tuber cinereum, mamillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, oculomotor nerve.

questions.text: Borders of open medulla:
questions.explanation: The open medulla's borders are defined by the medullary striae marking the base (floor of fourth ventricle), the apex continuous with the central canal, and the hypoglossal, vagal, and vestibular trigones forming the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Open medulla borders: striae at base, central canal at apex, trigones as floor.
questions.modelAnswer: Base: medullary striae; Apex: continuous with central canal; Floor: hypoglossal, vagal, and vestibular trigones.

questions.text: GSE column nuclei:
questions.explanation: General somatic efferent (GSE) cranial nerve nuclei include the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), abducent (CN VI), and hypoglossal (CN XII) nuclei supplying extraocular and tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: GSE column nuclei: CN 3, 4, 6, 12.
questions.modelAnswer: General somatic efferent (GSE) cranial nerve nuclei include the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), abducent (CN VI), and hypoglossal (CN XII) nuclei supplying extraocular and tongue muscles.

questions.text: SVE column nuclei:
questions.explanation: Special visceral efferent (SVE) nuclei include the motor nucleus of trigeminal (CN V), motor nucleus of facial (CN VII), and nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X, XI) supplying branchial arch-derived muscles.
questions.keyConcept: SVE column nuclei: motor nuclei of CN 5, 7, and nucleus ambiguus (9,10,11).
questions.modelAnswer: Motor nucleus of 5, Motor nucleus of 7, Nucleus ambiguus (9,10,11).

questions.text: GVE column nuclei:
questions.explanation: General visceral efferent (GVE) nuclei include the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III for pupil constriction), superior salivatory (CN VII), inferior salivatory (CN IX), and dorsal vagal nuclei (CN X).
questions.keyConcept: GVE column nuclei: Edinger-Westphal, superior/inferior salivatory, dorsal vagal.
questions.modelAnswer: Edinger‑Westphal (3), Superior salivatory (7), Inferior salivatory (9), Dorsal vagal (10).

questions.text: Muscles supplied by motor nucleus of trigeminal:
questions.explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve supplies the four muscles of mastication plus tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and the anterior belly of digastric.
questions.keyConcept: Motor V supplies mastication muscles, tensor tympani/palate, mylohyoid, anterior digastric.
questions.modelAnswer: 4 muscles of mastication, Tensor palate, Tensor tympani, Anterior belly of digastric, Mylohyoid.

questions.text: Arteries supplying medulla:
questions.explanation: The medulla receives blood from the anterior spinal artery, PICA (the largest branch), and direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, with additional contribution from posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Medulla supplied by anterior spinal, PICA, vertebral branches, and posterior spinal arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal, PICA, medullary branches of vertebral, posterior spinal.

questions.text: Fracture of anterior cranial fossa:
questions.explanation: Anterior cranial fossa fractures typically tear the cribriform plate, causing CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia; blood tracks into orbital contents producing subconjunctival hemorrhage and orbital ecchymosis.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior fossa fracture: CSF rhinorrhea, subconjunctival and orbital hemorrhage.
questions.modelAnswer: Bleeding and CSF rhinorrhea, orbital hemorrhage and subconjunctival hemorrhage.

questions.text: Fracture of middle cranial fossa:
questions.explanation: Middle cranial fossa fractures frequently involve the petrous temporal bone, causing CSF otorrhea, Battle sign (mastoid bruising), and commonly affecting CN VII and VIII with facial paralysis and hearing loss.
questions.keyConcept: Middle fossa fracture: CSF otorrhea, Battle sign, CN 7 and 8 involvement.
questions.modelAnswer: Bleeding and CSF otorrhea, CN 7 & 8 involvement.

questions.text: Attachments of falx cerebri:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri attaches superiorly to the crista galli and frontal crest, posteriorly to the tentorium's upper surface, along its upper border to the sagittal sulcus lips, and its free lower border encloses the inferior sagittal sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri attachments: crista galli, tentorium, sagittal sulcus, inferior sagittal sinus.
questions.modelAnswer: Apex: crista galli and frontal crest; Base: upper surface of tentorium; Upper border: lips of sagittal sulcus; Lower free border: encloses inferior sagittal sinus.

questions.text: Attachments of falx cerebelli:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebelli attaches along its base to the tentorium cerebelli, at its apex to the foramen magnum margins, along its posterior border to the internal occipital crest, and is free anteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebelli: tentorium base, foramen magnum apex, occipital crest posteriorly, free anteriorly.
questions.modelAnswer: Base: tentorium; Apex: margins of foramen magnum; Posterior border: internal occipital crest; Anterior border: free.

questions.text: Paired sinuses:
questions.explanation: The paired dural sinuses include sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, and transverse sinuses, occurring on both sides of the cranial cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Paired sinuses: sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior/inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.
questions.modelAnswer: Sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.

questions.text: Nerve piercing cribriform plate:
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve (CN I) consists of special sensory fibers that pierce the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to reach the olfactory bulb from the nasal mucosa, making it unique among cranial nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory nerve pierces cribriform plate to reach olfactory bulb.
questions.modelAnswer: The olfactory nerve (CN I) passes through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The filaments of CN I traverse the foramina in the cribriform plate to reach the olfactory bulb. Fractures here can cause anosmia and CSF rhinorrhea.

questions.text: Nerve through optic canal:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve (CN II) passes through the optic canal, carrying visual information from the retina to the lateral geniculate body, making it functionally part of the CNS rather than a true peripheral nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve (CN II) traverses the optic canal.
questions.modelAnswer: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery. The central retinal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery that enters the optic nerve. The ophthalmic artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery at the lateral aspect of the optic chiasma.

questions.text: Nerve in front of crossing of tentorium margins:
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges in the interpeduncular fossa, anterior to the crossing of the tentorium margins, before dividing into superior and inferior branches that enter the orbit.
questions.keyConcept: Oculomotor nerve emerges anterior to tentorium crossing.
questions.modelAnswer: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) runs in the interpeduncular fossa, in front of the tentorial edge (tentorium cerebelli crossing). It exits the brainstem between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, entering the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus just below the trochlear nerve.

questions.text: Nerve at crossing of tentorium margins:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as the only cranial nerve to exit posteriorly from the dorsal midbrain, crossing at the superior medullary velum at the tentorium margin level.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve exits posteriorly at tentorium crossing level.
questions.modelAnswer: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the smallest cranial nerve and exits the brainstem at the dorsal surface of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus. It wraps around the cerebral peduncle and runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, anterior to CN III at the tentorial edge.

questions.text: Nerve through hypoglossal canal:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal, which lies above the foramen magnum, carrying motor fibers to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve passes through hypoglossal canal above foramen magnum.
questions.modelAnswer: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal (anterior condylar canal) of the occipital bone. It exits the skull to supply the intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, mediating tongue movements and shape changes for speech and swallowing.

questions.text: Boundaries of temporal fossa:
questions.explanation: The temporal fossa is bounded superiorly by the superior temporal line and inferiorly by the zygomatic arch, with the deep temporal fascia separating it from the temporalis muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Temporal fossa: superior temporal line above, zygomatic arch below.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: superior temporal line; Inferior: zygomatic arch.

questions.text: Boundaries of infratemporal fossa:
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa is bounded laterally by the mandibular ramus, medially by the lateral pterygoid plate, anteriorly by the posterior maxilla, posteriorly by the styloid process, and superiorly by the greater wing of sphenoid.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa boundaries: mandible laterally, pterygoid plate medially, maxilla anteriorly, styloid posteriorly.
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral: ramus of mandible; Medial: lateral pterygoid plate; Anterior: posterior maxilla; Posterior: styloid process; Superior: greater wing of sphenoid.

questions.text: Communications of infratemporal fossa:
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa communicates superiorly with the middle cranial fossa via foramen ovale and spinosum, anteriorly with the orbit via inferior orbital fissure, medially with the pterygopalatine fossa via pterygomaxillary fissure, and with the temporal fossa deep to the zygomatic arch.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa communicates: middle cranial fossa, orbit, pterygopalatine fossa, temporal fossa.
questions.modelAnswer: With temporal fossa (deep to zygomatic arch); With middle cranial fossa (foramen ovale & spinosum); With orbit (inferior orbital fissure); With pterygopalatine fossa (pterygomaxillary fissure).

questions.text: Nerve supply of muscles of mastication:
questions.explanation: All muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid) are innervated by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3), except the medial pterygoid which receives a branch from the trunk.
questions.keyConcept: Muscles of mastication: all by anterior division of V3 except medial pterygoid (trunk).
questions.modelAnswer: All by anterior division of mandibular nerve except medial pterygoid by trunk.

questions.text: Actions of muscles of mastication:
questions.explanation: The muscles of mastication produce protrusion (lateral pterygoid, medial pterygoid, masseter) except temporalis which retracts; elevation is produced by all except lateral pterygoid which depresses; medial and lateral pterygoid together produce side-to-side grinding movements.
questions.keyConcept: Mastication actions: protrusion (except temporalis), elevation (except lateral pterygoid), side-to-side movement.
questions.modelAnswer: All protrude except temporalis retracts; All elevate except lateral pterygoid depresses; Medial & lateral pterygoid produce side‑to‑side movement.

questions.text: Lateral relations of lateral pterygoid:
questions.explanation: Structures lateral to the lateral pterygoid include the ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, and pterygoid venous plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral relations of lateral pterygoid: mandible, medial pterygoid, temporalis tendon, maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus.
questions.modelAnswer: Ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus.

questions.text: Medial relations of lateral pterygoid:
questions.explanation: Medial to the lateral pterygoid lie the deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palati muscle, middle meningeal artery, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, and sphenomandibular ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Medial relations of lateral pterygoid: medial pterygoid, tensor palati, MMA, V3 trunk, otic ganglion.
questions.modelAnswer: Deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palati, MMA, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, sphenomandibular ligament.

questions.text: 3 ligaments of TMJ:
questions.explanation: The three ligaments associated with the TMJ are the lateral ligament (thickening of joint capsule), stylomandibular ligament (from styloid to mandible), and sphenomandibular ligament (from spine to lingula).
questions.keyConcept: TMJ ligaments: lateral, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular.
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular.

questions.text: Branches of posterior division of mandibular nerve:
questions.explanation: The posterior division of the mandibular nerve gives three branches: auriculotemporal (sensory to temple and ear), lingual (sensory to anterior two-thirds of tongue), and inferior alveolar (sensory to lower teeth and chin).
questions.keyConcept: Posterior V3 branches: auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar.
questions.modelAnswer: Auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar.

questions.text: Branches of inferior alveolar nerve:
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives off the mylohyoid branch before entering the mandibular foramen, then continues as the mental nerve (exiting mental foramen) and incisive nerve (supplying lower anterior teeth).
questions.keyConcept: Inferior alveolar branches: mylohyoid, mental, incisive nerves.
questions.modelAnswer: The inferior alveolar nerve (branch of V3) gives off: (1) Mylohyoid nerve — motor to mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric; (2) Dental branches — to mandibular teeth; (3) Incisive nerve — to mandibular premolars, canine, and incisors; (4) Mental nerve — exits mental foramen to chin and lower lip.

questions.text: 4 branches of maxillary nerve:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off a meningeal branch, two ganglionic branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion, the zygomatic nerve, and the posterior superior alveolar nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve branches: meningeal, two ganglionic, zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal, two ganglionic, zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.

questions.text: Boundaries of pterygopalatine fossa:
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa is bounded anteriorly by the posterior maxilla, posteriorly by the pterygoid process, medially by the palatine bone, and laterally it opens into the infratemporal fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa: maxilla anterior, pterygoid posterior, palatine medial, open laterally.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: posterior maxilla; Posterior: pterygoid process; Medial: palatine bone; Lateral: opens to infratemporal fossa.

questions.text: Contents of pterygopalatine fossa:
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa contains the third part of the maxillary artery, branches of the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion with associated autonomic connections.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa contents: maxillary artery part 3, maxillary nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion.
questions.modelAnswer: 3rd part of maxillary artery, maxillary nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.text: Branches of 3rd part of maxillary artery:
questions.explanation: The third (pterygopalatine) part of the maxillary artery gives posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater and lesser palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal branches, and the artery of the pterygoid canal.
questions.keyConcept: Third maxillary artery: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, pterygoid canal.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater & lesser palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, artery of pterygoid canal.

questions.text: Drainage of pterygoid plexus:
questions.explanation: The pterygoid venous plexus drains into the maxillary vein, which then joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein, ultimately connecting to the external jugular system.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus drains to maxillary vein.
questions.modelAnswer: The pterygoid plexus drains into the retromandibular vein via the maxillary vein, which joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein. It also communicates with the facial vein via the deep facial vein and drains into the cavernous sinus via emissary veins.

questions.text: Otic ganglion:
questions.explanation: The otic ganglion sits below the foramen ovale; its parasympathetic root comes from the inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic branch of CN IX, tympanic plexus, and lesser petrosal nerve; it distributes to the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Otic ganglion: below foramen ovale; parasympathetic from inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic plexus to parotid.
questions.modelAnswer: Site: below foramen ovale; Sympathetic root: around MMA; Parasympathetic root: inferior salivatory nucleus → tympanic branch of 9 → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion; Distribution: postganglionic to parotid.

questions.text: Compare sympathetic root:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic roots differ by ganglion: otic ganglion receives fibers around the middle meningeal artery, submandibular ganglion around the facial artery, and sphenopalatine ganglion around the internal carotid artery via the deep petrosal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic roots: otic (MMA), submandibular (facial artery), sphenopalatine (ICA/deep petrosal).
questions.modelAnswer: Otic: around MMA; Submandibular: around facial artery; Sphenopalatine: around ICA (deep petrosal).

questions.text: Tributaries of external jugular vein:
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein receives tributaries including the anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular veins, draining superficial structures of the head and neck.
questions.keyConcept: EJV tributaries: anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.

questions.text: Boundaries of digastric triangle:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle boundaries are: anterior belly of digastric, posterior belly of digastric with stylohyoid, and the inferior border of mandible to mastoid; the floor is formed by mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle: anterior/posterior bellies of digastric, mandible to mastoid; floor mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: anterior belly of digastric; Posterior: posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid; Superior: inferior border of mandible to mastoid; Roof: skin, superficial, deep fascia; Floor: mylohyoid and hyoglossus.

questions.text: 5 contents of digastric triangle:
questions.explanation: Five contents of the digastric triangle are the submandibular gland, submandibular lymph nodes, submandibular ganglion (parasympathetic), facial artery, and facial vein.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle contents: submandibular gland, LN, ganglion, facial artery and vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Submandibular gland, submandibular LN, submandibular ganglion, facial artery, facial vein.

questions.text: Contents of muscular triangle:
questions.explanation: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid (strap) muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid, which stabilize the larynx and hyoid during swallowing and speech.
questions.keyConcept: Muscular triangle contains infrahyoid strap muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: The contents of the muscular triangle include: (1) Sternothyroid and sternohyoid muscles (forming the floor); (2) Superior thyroid artery; (3) Superior laryngeal nerve and its branches (internal and external laryngeal nerves); (4) Lymph nodes and the thyroid gland.

questions.text: Cervical sympathetic ganglia sites:
questions.explanation: The three paired cervical sympathetic ganglia are positioned at specific vertebral levels: superior ganglion at C2-3, middle ganglion at C6-7, and inferior ganglion (often fused with T1 as stellate ganglion) at C7 level.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical sympathetic ganglia: superior (C2-3), middle (C6-7), inferior (C7).
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: C2-3; Middle: C6-7; Inferior: C7.

questions.text: The pterion is a clinically important landmark because it overlies the:
questions.explanation: The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery, making it a critical landmark as fractures here can cause epidural hemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
options: Anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery

questions.text: The second order neuron for pain and temperature from the face is located in the:
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature sensation from the face is carried by the trigeminal nerve to the spinal nucleus of V (caudal part), which is the second-order neuron for this pathway before crossing to the contralateral side.
questions.keyConcept: Pain/temperature from face: second-order neuron in spinal nucleus of V.

questions.text: A patient has difficulty initiating movement, resting tremor, and cogwheel rigidity. Which structure is primarily affected?
questions.explanation: Parkinsonism features (difficulty initiating movement, resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity) result from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonism: substantia nigra degeneration.

questions.text: In a complete spinal cord transection at the level of T6, which of the following would be expected?
questions.explanation: A complete transection at T6 would cause paraplegia (paralysis of both lower limbs) since this level is below the cervical region and does not affect upper limb innervation or respiratory muscles.
questions.keyConcept: T6 transection: paraplegia of both lower limbs.
options: Loss of pain sensation from the upper limbs

questions.text: A lesion of the left optic tract causes:
questions.explanation: A left optic tract lesion causes right homonymous hemianopia because optic tract fibers carry information from the contralateral visual field, so damage affects the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Left optic tract lesion: right homonymous hemianopia.

questions.text: The maxillary nerve exits the skull through which foramen?
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) exits the skull through the foramen rotundum, passing from the middle cranial fossa into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve exits via foramen rotundum.

questions.text: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the medulla oblongata, receiving input from the spinal cord and cerebral cortex and sending climbing fiber projections to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary nucleus: located in medulla oblongata.

questions.text: The medial geniculate body is part of the auditory pathway and receives input from the:
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body receives input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus, serving as the thalamic relay for the auditory pathway to the auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body receives input from inferior colliculus.

questions.text: A patient with a tumour in the left frontal eye field (area 8) will have difficulty:
questions.explanation: The left frontal eye field (area 8) controls conjugate gaze to the right by sending signals that move both eyes rightward; a lesion here causes difficulty gazing to the contralateral (right) side.
questions.keyConcept: Left frontal eye field controls gaze to the right (contralateral).

questions.text: The sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the spinal cord at levels:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord from T1 to L2 levels, representing the thoracolumbar outflow of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons: T1-L2 (thoracolumbar outflow).

questions.text: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) coordinates movements between which structures?
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) connects the vestibular nuclei to the abducens and oculomotor nuclei, coordinating eye movements with head movements in the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
questions.keyConcept: MLF coordinates eyes and head via vestibulo-ocular reflex.

questions.text: A patient develops contralateral loss of pain and temperature of the body with ipsilateral facial signs. The occluded vessel is the:
questions.explanation: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral pain and temperature loss below lesion: lateral spinothalamic tract lesion.
options: Superior cerebellar artery supplying the upper cerebellum

questions.text: The motor branch to mylohyoid arises from the posterior division of the mandibular nerve as the:
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives the (motor) nerve to mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Motor branch to mylohyoid arises from posterior division of mandibular nerve (V3).

questions.text: The first-order neuron carrying pain and temperature from the face lies in the:
questions.explanation: Cell bodies are in the trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Pain and temperature first-order neuron: pseudounipolar cell body in trigeminal ganglion.
options: Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

questions.text: On the medial surface of the infratemporal fossa lies the:
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid plate forms the medial wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid muscle lies on medial surface of infratemporal fossa.

questions.text: The chief retractor of the mandible is the:
questions.explanation: Posterior temporalis fibers retract the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis is the chief retractor of mandible.

questions.text: Unconscious proprioception from the upper limb (elbow/wrist) is carried by the:
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from upper limb to cerebellum.

questions.text: A patient shows ipsilateral tongue atrophy, contralateral loss of vibration, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature of the body. The lesion is in the:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (CN XII, medial lemniscus, pyramid).
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviation toward lesion with ipsilateral atrophy: hypoglossal nerve lesion.

questions.text: Retrolentiform part of internal capsule DOESN'T transmit:
questions.explanation: The retrolentiform part of internal capsule contains visual radiation, occipito-pontine, and parieto-pontine fibers, but the auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part.
questions.keyConcept: Retrolentiform: visual/occipito-parieto-pontine fibers; auditory goes sublentiform.

questions.text: Inability to perform tasks although the person has the will to perform it indicates a lesion in ……… area.
questions.explanation: A premotor area lesion causes apraxia - inability to perform tasks despite intact motor pathways and will, due to loss of motor planning programs.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor lesion: apraxia (can't perform tasks despite will).

questions.text: Inability to recognize familiar objects by touch indicates a lesion in:
questions.explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) results from lesions in the superior parietal lobule, which integrates sensory information for object recognition.
questions.keyConcept: Astereognosis: superior parietal lobule lesion.

questions.text: Match the cortical area in column A with the result of lesion in column B.
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area lesion: word comprehension loss; primary auditory: decreased hearing; secondary auditory: sound understanding; frontal eye field: voluntary gaze loss; primary visual: hemianopia with macular sparing.
questions.keyConcept: Lesion effects: Wernicke (comprehension), 1ary auditory (hearing), 2ary auditory (sound meaning), eye field (gaze), 1ary visual (hemianopia).

pairs.target: Inability to understand written or spoken words.
Loss of voluntary conjugate eye movement.

questions.text: The occipitofrontalis muscle accounts for the ……… layer of the scalp.
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle forms the third (musculoaponeurotic) layer of the scalp, connecting the galea aponeurotica to the orbital margins.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis: third layer of scalp.

questions.text: Skin of the hairy area of the temple is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3) supplies the hairy temple area, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular division.
questions.keyConcept: Hairy temple: auriculotemporal nerve (V3).

questions.text: Skin over occipital bone up to the vertex is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The posterior primary rami (dorsal rami) of C2 and C3 supply the skin over the occipital bone up to the vertex, including the greater and lesser occipital nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital area: supplied by dorsal rami of C2 and C3.

questions.text: The anterior facial vein is formed by union of ……… veins.
questions.explanation: The anterior facial vein is formed by union of the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins at the medial angle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior facial vein: formed by supratrochlear and supraorbital veins.

questions.text: The common facial vein drains into the ……… vein.
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein after forming from the facial and anterior facial veins joining.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein: drains into internal jugular vein.

questions.text: A muscle covered by deep fascia is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is covered by thebuccal fascia (deep fascia), while orbicularis oculi and oris are covered by superficial fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: covered by deep fascia (buccal fascia).

questions.text: A muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch is:
questions.explanation: The masseter muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication and mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Masseter: first pharyngeal arch derivative.

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the orbicularis oculi muscle:
questions.explanation: The lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attaches behind the lacrimal sac (posterior to it), not in front, to compress and dilate the lacrimal sac.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi lacrimal part: attached behind lacrimal sac.
options: Its orbital part closes the eye tightly.
Its palpebral part closes the eye gently.
Its lacrimal part is attached in front of the lacrimal sac.
It develops from the second pharyngeal arch.

questions.text: An active muscle during whistling is:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle compresses and purses the lips during whistling, while buccinator muscle keeps food between teeth during chewing.
questions.keyConcept: Whistling: orbicularis oris contracts to purse lips.

questions.text: Accumulation of food in the vestibule of the mouth denotes weakness of ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: Buccinator weakness causes food accumulation in the vestibule because this muscle normally keeps food between the teeth during mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Food in vestibule: buccinator weakness.

questions.text: Pain from the lower eyelid is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) carries pain sensation from the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, exiting through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower eyelid pain: infraorbital nerve (V2).

questions.text: Ethmoidal arteries supply the cranial dura via ……… arteries.
questions.explanation: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from the ophthalmic artery) give off anterior meningeal arteries that supply the cranial dura in the anterior fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Ethmoidal arteries supply dura via anterior meningeal branches.

questions.text: All the following are true about the middle meningeal artery EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through foramen spinosum (not ovale), making it vulnerable to fractures in the temporal region causing epidural hematoma.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery: enters via foramen spinosum, not ovale.
options: It is the largest meningeal artery.
It is a branch from 1st part of maxillary artery.
It enters the cranial cavity through foramen ovale.
It gives frontal and parietal terminal branches.

questions.text: Which of the following diploic veins drains extracranially?
questions.explanation: The frontal diploic vein drains through the supraorbital notch to the supraorbital vein and eventually the angular vein, providing extracranial drainage.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal diploic vein drains extracranially via supraorbital vein.

questions.text: All the following are tributaries of external jugular vein EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein, not the external jugular. The external jugular tributaries are anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein drains internal jugular, not external jugular.

questions.text: The only tributary of the subclavian vein is:
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is the only named tributary of the subclavian vein, carrying blood from the superficial structures of the head and neck.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein: only named tributary of subclavian vein.

questions.text: The viscera of the neck are surrounded by ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The pretracheal fascia forms a sheath around the trachea, esophagus, and thyroid gland, fusing laterally with the carotid sheath.
questions.keyConcept: Pretracheal fascia surrounds cervical viscera.

questions.text: The retropharyngeal space lies:
questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering pharynx/esophagus) anteriorly and prevertebral fascia posteriorly, extending from skull base to T1.
questions.keyConcept: Retropharyngeal space: between buccopharyngeal and prevertebral fascia.

questions.text: The axillary sheath is an extension from ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is an extension of the prevertebral fascia (from the anterior vertebral muscles) that surrounds the axillary vessels and brachial plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Axillary sheath: extension of prevertebral fascia.

questions.text: A nerve running along the posterior border of sternomastoid muscle is:
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve runs along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle, arising from C2 ventral ramus to supply the scalp behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve: posterior border of SCM.

questions.text: The subclavian artery is divided into 3 parts by ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: The anterior scalene muscle divides the subclavian artery into three parts: first (posterior to scalene), second (behind scalene), and third (lateral to scalene).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery divided by anterior scalene muscle into 3 parts.

questions.text: Tight scalene muscles can compress:
questions.explanation: Tight scalene muscles (especially anterior and middle) can compress the subclavian artery and brachial plexus in the costoclavicular space, causing thoracic outlet syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Scalene tightness compresses subclavian artery.

questions.text: A muscle DOESN'T share in boundaries of the suboccipital triangle is:
questions.explanation: The rectus capitis posterior minor does NOT form boundaries of the suboccipital triangle - only rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior, and obliquus capitis inferior do.
questions.keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle: rectus major, obliquus superior/inferior (NOT rectus minor).

questions.text: A nerve seen in the floor of the suboccipital triangle is:
questions.explanation: The dorsal ramus of C1 (suboccipital nerve) emerges in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, providing motor innervation to suboccipital muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle floor: dorsal ramus of C1.

questions.text: Which of the following lies superficial to temporalis fascia?
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve lies superficial to the temporalis fascia as it ascends toward the temple, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve: superficial to temporalis fascia.

questions.text: A muscle acting as a powerful retractor of the mandible is:
questions.explanation: The temporalis muscle is a powerful retractor of the mandible, pulling the mandibular condyle backward to close the mouth after opening.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis: powerful retractor of mandible.

questions.text: The mandibular nerve reaches the infratemporal fossa through foramen:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) passes from the middle cranial fossa to the infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve enters infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.

questions.text: The trunk of the mandibular nerve supplies ……… muscle(s).
questions.explanation: The trunk of the mandibular nerve gives off medial pterygoid nerve (supplying medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, and tensor palati) before dividing into anterior and posterior divisions.
questions.keyConcept: V3 trunk supplies: medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, tensor palati.

questions.text: Middle meningeal artery is encircled by roots of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve encircles the middle meningeal artery with its two roots, forming a neural loop around the vessel in the infratemporal fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve encircles middle meningeal artery.

questions.text: Bad extraction of lower 3rd molar tooth may cause loss of sensations from:
questions.explanation: Bad extraction of lower third molar can damage the inferior alveolar nerve (running in the mandibular canal), causing anesthesia of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Lower 3rd molar extraction: possible lingual nerve damage (anterior 2/3 tongue).

questions.text: To operate on the lower teeth, the ……… nerve is anaesthetized.
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (branch of V3) is anesthetized for lower teeth operations, injected near the mandibular foramen on the medial aspect of the ramus.
questions.keyConcept: Lower teeth surgery: inferior alveolar nerve anesthetized.

questions.text: A branch from the 3rd part of maxillary artery is:
questions.explanation: The posterior superior alveolar artery is a branch of the third part of maxillary artery that supplies the upper molars and sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior superior alveolar artery: branch of maxillary artery part 3.

questions.text: A nerve passing between the 2 heads of lateral pterygoid muscle is:
questions.explanation: The buccal nerve passes between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle to reach the buccinator muscle, carrying sensory fibers to the cheek.
questions.keyConcept: Buccal nerve passes between two heads of lateral pterygoid.

questions.text: Fracture of neck of mandible can lead to injury of all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The masseteric nerve runs on the lateral surface of the mandibular neck, so it can be injured in fractures; the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves are also at risk, but auriculotemporal is not typically affected.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular neck fracture: masseteric, lingual, inferior alveolar nerves at risk.

questions.text: Maxillary nerve reaches the pterygopalatine fossa through foramen:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) passes from the middle cranial fossa through foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve reaches pterygopalatine fossa through foramen rotundum.

questions.text: Pain from upper canine teeth is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The upper canine teeth are supplied by the anterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of infraorbital nerve, V2), which also supplies the upper incisors.
questions.keyConcept: Upper canine: anterior superior alveolar nerve (V2).

questions.text: The skin of the prominence of cheek is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the skin over the cheek prominence (zygomatic area), a branch of V2 via the zygomatic nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Cheek prominence: zygomaticotemporal nerve (V2).

questions.text: Nerve of pterygoid canal is formed by union of ……… nerves.
questions.explanation: The nerve of pterygoid canal (Vidians nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic from CN VII) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic from carotid plexus).
questions.keyConcept: Nerve of pterygoid canal: greater petrosal + deep petrosal nerves.

questions.text: Deviation of the uvula to the right side denotes injury of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The uvula deviates AWAY from the lesioned side due to weakness of the palatine muscles on the affected side. Deviation to the right indicates left vagus (CN X) injury.
questions.keyConcept: Uvula deviates AWAY from lesioned side (CN X motor).

questions.text: The jugular foramen transmits all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, XI, and the inferior petrosal sinus. The hypoglossal nerve passes through its own canal (hypoglossal canal) separately.
questions.keyConcept: Jugular foramen: CN 9,10,11, inferior petrosal sinus (not hypoglossal).

questions.text: Difficulty in protruding the tongue with its deviation to the right side denotes injury of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: Tongue deviation toward the right side during protrusion indicates right hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury, as the unaffected genioglossus pulls the tongue toward the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviates TOWARD lesioned hypoglossal nerve side.

questions.text: The parasympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion is ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion is the chorda tympani nerve (branch of CN VII carrying parasympathetic to submandibular and sublingual glands).
questions.keyConcept: Submandibular ganglion parasympathetic root: chorda tympani (CN VII).

questions.text: The ……… nerve suspends the pterygopalatine ganglion in its place.
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion is suspended by the maxillary nerve (V2) which provides its sensory roots passing through without synapsing.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve suspends pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.text: A branch from the 2nd part of subclavian artery is:
questions.explanation: The second part of subclavian artery gives rise to the internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk (supplying thyroid, neck, and chest wall structures).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery part 2: internal thoracic and thyrocervical trunk.

questions.text: The common carotid artery divides at the level of ……… vertebrae.
questions.explanation: The common carotid artery typically bifurcates at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4 vertebral level).
questions.keyConcept: Common carotid bifurcates at upper border of thyroid cartilage (C4).

questions.text: All the following drain into the internal jugular vein EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein; other veins like inferior thyroid, middle thyroid, and vertebral vein also drain into the IJV.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein drains INTO internal jugular (so it doesn't drain external jugular).

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the subclavian vein:
questions.explanation: The subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to the anterior scalene muscle (not posterior), making it vulnerable to compression during clavicle fractures.
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to anterior scalene.
options: It is the continuation of the axillary vein.
It is separated from subclavian artery by anterior scalene muscle.
It grooves the 1st rib posterior to scalene tubercle.
It receives the external jugular vein.

questions.text: An abscess in the center of lower lip may cause enlargement of ……… lymph nodes.
questions.explanation: An abscess in the lower lip drains to the submandibular lymph nodes due to lymphatic drainage patterns of the anterior face.
questions.keyConcept: Lower lip abscess: submandibular lymph nodes enlarge.

questions.text: One of the following mandibular ligaments is a remnant of cartilage of the 1st pharyngeal arch:
questions.explanation: The sphenomandibular ligament is the remnant of Meckel's cartilage (first pharyngeal arch cartilage), stretching from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenomandibular ligament: remnant of 1st pharyngeal arch cartilage.

questions.text: Rotation of the head to say "No" occurs at ……… joint.
questions.explanation: Saying 'No' involves rotation of the head at the atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2), where the dens of the axis articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas.
questions.keyConcept: Saying no: rotation at atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2).

questions.text: A muscle develops from the pharyngeal arch is:
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: second pharyngeal arch derivative.

questions.text: The lower lip is derived from:
questions.explanation: The lower lip is derived from the mandibular prominence (frontonasal process gives upper lip philtrum and maxilla), with lateral portions from the maxillary prominence.
questions.keyConcept: Lower lip: derived from mandibular prominence.

questions.text: The inter-maxillary segment gives all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The intermaxillary segment (primary palate) gives rise to the premaxilla, primary palate, and four incisor teeth. The center of the lower lip comes from the mandibular prominence, not the intermaxillary segment.
questions.keyConcept: Intermaxillary segment: premaxilla, primary palate, incisors (NOT secondary palate).
options: Sockets of the upper 4 incisor teeth.

questions.text: The upper part of the cheeks is derived from ……… prominence.
questions.explanation: The upper part of the cheeks is derived from the maxillary prominence (second pharyngeal arch), which also forms the upper lip lateral portions and secondary palate.
questions.keyConcept: Upper cheek: maxillary prominence.

questions.text: Excessive fusion between maxillary and mandibular prominences causes:
questions.explanation: Fusion of maxillary and mandibular prominences in utero causes microstomia (small mouth) or aglossia (absent tongue) if severe.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary-mandibular fusion: microstomia or aglossia.

questions.text: Abnormal early closure of coronal suture leads to:
questions.explanation: Early closure of the coronal suture causes brachycephaly (shortened anteroposterior skull diameter) due to compensatory growth in other directions.
questions.keyConcept: Coronal suture early closure: brachycephaly.

questions.text: Match the muscle in column A with its main action in column B.
questions.explanation: Matching pairs: Masseter elevates mandible, Temporalis retracts mandible, Medial pterygoid elevates and protrudes, Lateral pterygoid protrudes and opens, Digastric opens mouth, Buccinator compresses cheeks.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle actions: masseter elevate, temporalis retract, pterygoids protrude, digastric open, buccinator compress.

pairs.target: B) Lateral flexion of the skull.

questions.text: The branch of facial nerve that supplies the platysma is the:
questions.explanation: The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) descends into the neck to supply the platysma muscle. The temporal, zygomatic, and buccal branches supply facial muscles above the mouth.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical branch of facial nerve innervates the platysma

questions.text: In facial nerve lesion (Bell's palsy), all the following could be manifested EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is facial nerve (CN VII) palsy. It causes inability to close the eyelids and facial muscle weakness. Hearing is generally unaffected; in fact, sounds may seem louder (hyperacusis) due to stapedial nerve involvement.
questions.keyConcept: Bell's palsy does NOT cause weaker hearing; hyperacusis may occur due to stapedial nerve involvement
options: Falling of food out of mouth.

questions.text: Which of the following nerves that supply scalp & face is not derived of Trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) derives from the cervical plexus, not the trigeminal nerve. All other listed nerves are branches of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) is NOT a branch of the trigeminal nerve

questions.text: Describe branches of facial nerve in neck & its terminal branches.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve gives the posterior auricular nerve in the neck before entering the parotid gland. Its five terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. The cervical branch supplies the platysma.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical
questions.modelAnswer: The facial nerve gives off the posterior auricular nerve in the neck before entering the parotid gland. Within and beyond the parotid, it divides into five terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. The cervical branch supplies the platysma.

questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerves is attached to the back of the brain stem?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as the only cranial nerve to attach to the posterior (dorsal) surface of the brain stem. It emerges from the posterior aspect of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve is only CN from posterior brainstem

questions.text: A pontine cranial nerve that is not attached to lower border of pons:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is attached to the lateral surface of the pons, at the junction of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle. The abducent nerve attaches at the lower border, and facial/vestibulocochlear at the cerebellopontine angle.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal attaches at pons-middle cerebellar peduncle junction

questions.text: Rootlets of hypoglossal nerve lie:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve rootlets emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the pyramid and olive. This is the anterior surface of the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII between pyramid and olive
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons & pyramid.

questions.text: The cranial nerve that has the most medial attachment to the pons:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) has the most medial attachment to the pons, emerging in the median line at the pontomedullary junction. The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves attach more laterally.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial pontine attachment

questions.text: As regards cranial nerve attachment to brain stem, choose the CORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve attaches at the cerebellopontine angle, which is the angle between the pons, cerebellum, and medulla. This is the correct matching for the anatomical location.
questions.keyConcept: CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle
options: Hypoglossal nerve - posterolateral sulcus of medulla.
Vagus nerve - groove between pyramid & olive.
Facial nerve - lower border of pons above pyramid.

questions.text: As regards the attachment of the cranial nerves to the brain stem, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve attaches in the sulcus between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle. This is a posterior attachment, not between pyramid and olive. The statement is incorrect about the groove location.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII between olive and ICP
options: Hypoglossal nerve - sulcus between olive & ICP.
Trigeminal nerve - Junction of MCP & basis pontis.
Oculomotor nerve - medial side of crus cerebri.

questions.text: The cranial nerve nucleus that supplies muscles of the larynx is the:
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius is the visceral afferent column (receiving taste and visceral sensation), not the GVE column. GVE nuclei include Edinger-Westphal (III), superior/inferior salivary nuclei (VII/IX), and dorsal motor nucleus of X.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius is visceral afferent, not efferent

questions.text: The common motor nucleus of IX, X and XI cranial nerves is:
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It gives rise to special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) fibers that supply pharyngeal arch muscles (stylopharyngeus via IX, pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles via X, sternocleidomastoid and trapezius via XI).
questions.keyConcept: SVE column - pharyngeal arch muscles

questions.text: The mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve has the following functional component:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is the only nucleus in the CNS that contains pseudounipolar sensory neuron cell bodies. It carries proprioceptive impulses from muscles of mastication and other structures, making it a General Somatic Afferent (GSA) nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial longitudinal bundle coordinates vestibular-eye reflexes

questions.text: The parasympathetic nucleus of the ninth cranial nerve is the:
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the inferior salivatory nucleus. It provides parasympathetic preganglionic fibers to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: SVE column supplies pharyngeal arch muscles

questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerve nuclei is not connected to the medial longitudinal bundle:
questions.explanation: This matching tests cranial nerve nuclei columns: SE - somatic muscles (III,IV,VI,XII); SVE - pharyngeal arch muscles (V,VII,IX,X,XI); GVE - parasympathetic (III,VII,IX,X).
questions.keyConcept: SVE column supplies pharyngeal arch derived muscles

questions.text: All the following are nuclei of facial nerve EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord: anterior horn, lateral horn, and anterior/lateral white columns. It does NOT supply the posterior columns.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal does not supply posterior columns
