questions.text: The pharyngeal arch supplied by the only pontine cranial nerve that is NOT attached to the lower border of pons is:
questions.explanation: The medial zone of medulla containing the pyramid is supplied by the anterior spinal artery, which runs in the anterior median fissure. This zone includes the pyramid and medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies medial medulla

questions.text: First neuron for proprioception from muscles of mastication is:
questions.explanation: The posterior columns (gracile and cuneate nuclei) are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries and vertebral arteries, NOT by the anterior spinal artery. The anterior spinal supplies the anterior 2/3 of the cord.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior columns not supplied by anterior spinal artery

questions.text: For each type of cranial nerve nuclei columns in left column, choose the appropriate structure supplied by it in right column:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerve nuclei are organized into columns: Somatic Efferent (eye/tongue muscles), Special Visceral Efferent (pharyngeal arch muscles), General Visceral Efferent (parasympathetic), and Visceral Afferent (taste/visceral sensation).
questions.keyConcept: Cranial nerve nuclei organized into functional columns

questions.text: For each type of cranial nerve nuclei columns in left column, choose the appropriate function from right column:
questions.explanation: Each nucleus column has distinct functions: SE controls voluntary eye/tongue movement; SVE controls mastication/facial expression/swallowing; GVE controls parasympathetic functions; Visceral afferent handles taste and visceral sensation.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus columns have distinct functional roles

pairs.target: Supplies muscles that develop from myotomes.
Supplies muscles that develop from pharyngeal arches.

questions.text: Describe ventral surface of medulla oblongata & cranial nerves attached to it.
questions.explanation: The ventral surface of the medulla oblongata shows: (1) PYRAMIDS - containing corticospinal fibers, located on either side of anterior median fissure; (2) OLVES (inferior olivary nuclei) - lateral to pyramids; (3) CRANIAL NERVES: CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus), CN XI (accessory - cranial part), and CN XII (hypoglossal) attach at the pontomedullary junction. The pyramids are most prominent features and are where pyramidal decussation occurs caudally.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral medulla: pyramids, olives, and cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII attached at pontomedullary junction
questions.modelAnswer: LEMNISCI (sensory pathways in brainstem): (1) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS - from dorsal column nuclei (gracile/cuneate) through medulla, pons, midbrain to VPL thalamus; carries conscious proprioception and fine touch. (2) SPINAL LEMNISCUS - from spinothalamic tracts through brainstem to VPL; carries pain and temperature. (3) TRIGEMINAL LEMNISCUS - from trigeminal sensory nuclei to VPM thalamus; carries face sensation. (4) LATERAL LEMNISCUS - auditory pathway from cochlear nuclei to inferior colliculus.

questions.text: Describe ventral surface of pons & cranial nerves attached to it.
questions.explanation: The ventral surface of the pons shows: (1) BASILAR SULCUS - midline groove containing basilar artery; (2) TRANSVERSE FIBERS - connecting the two hemispheres of cerebellum; (3) CRANIAL NERVES: CN V (trigeminal) attaches at the lateral aspect of the pons; CN VI (abducens), CN VII (facial), and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) attach at the pontomedullary junction. The pons is divided into basilar part (ventral) and tegmental part (dorsal).
questions.keyConcept: Ventral pons: basilar sulcus, transverse fibers, CN V at lateral surface, CN VI-VIII at pontomedullary junction
questions.modelAnswer: INTERNAL FEATURES OF MEDULLA: (1) PYRAMIDS - contain corticospinal fibers; (2) OLVES - contain inferior olivary nuclei; (3) INTERNAL ARCUATE FIBERS - decussating sensory fibers from dorsal column nuclei; (4) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS - formed after sensory decussation; (5) HYPOGLOSSAL NUCLEUS - in floor near central canal; (6) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS OF X; (7) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS; (8) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS; (9) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS; (10) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLES laterally.

questions.text: Describe ventral surface of midbrain & cranial nerves attached to it.
questions.explanation: The ventral surface of the midbrain shows the cerebral peduncles (crura cerebri): two cylindrical masses separated by the interpeduncular fossa. CN III (oculomotor) emerges from the medial surface of each peduncle. The peduncles contain descending motor fibers. The midbrain connects the pons (below) to the diencephalon (above). The ventral midbrain is separated from the dorsal tectum by the cerebral aqueduct.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral midbrain: cerebral peduncles with CN III emerging medially; connects pons to diencephalon
questions.modelAnswer: PYRAMID AL DECUSSATION: (LOCATION) Caudal medulla; (PROCESS) About 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross obliquely in the anterior median fissure; (RESULT) Crossed fibers form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral white column; uncrossed fibers remain as anterior corticospinal tract; (CLINICAL) Decussation explains contralateral motor control and UMN lesion signs.

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of facial nerve & the structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: Nuclei of the facial nerve: (1) FACIAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (SVE) - motor to muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric; (2) SUPERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to lacrimal gland (via greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion), submandibular and sublingual glands (via chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion); (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA) - taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue via chorda tympani; (4) MESENCEPHALIC NUCLEUS OF V - proprioception from facial muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve nuclei: motor (facial expression muscles), superior salivary (lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands), solitarius (taste)
questions.modelAnswer: (Diagnosis) Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) thrombosis - lateral medullary syndrome. (Vertigo and nystagmus) Vestibular nuclei involvement; (Absence of pharyngeal reflex) Nucleus ambiguus; (Absence of gag reflex) Nucleus ambiguus involvement; (Horner syndrome) Descending sympathetic pathway in lateral medulla.

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of trigeminal nerve & structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) runs in the superior wall (roof) of the cavernous sinus, along with the oculomotor and abducent nerves. The ophthalmic nerve (V1) runs in the lateral wall.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV in superior wall of cavernous sinus
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF TRIGEMINAL NERVE: (1) MOTOR NUCLEUS (SVE) in pons → muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric; (2) PRINCIPAL SENSORY NUCLEUS (GSA) in pons → discriminative/light touch from face; (3) SPINAL NUCLEUS (GSA) in medulla → pain and temperature from face; (4) MESENCEPHALIC NUCLEUS in midbrain → proprioception from mastication muscles, teeth, TMJ.

questions.text: Sensory innervation to the dura above the tentorium cerebelli is from which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: Extradural hemorrhage results from rupture of the middle meningeal artery, which passes through the foramen spinosum and grooves the inner table of the skull at the pterion. This creates a lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery rupture causes extradural hemorrhage

questions.text: Describe roots of trigeminal nerve.
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve emerges from the pons by two roots: a large sensory root and a smaller motor root. The sensory root carries general somatic sensation from the face and contains the central processes of the trigeminal ganglion cells, while the motor root carries special visceral efferent fibers for muscles of mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal nerve has two roots: large sensory root and small motor root emerging from pons.
questions.modelAnswer: The trigeminal nerve emerges from the lateral aspect of the pons by two roots: (1) Sensory root—larger root carrying general somatic sensation (pain, temperature, touch, proprioception) from the face and oral cavity. It contains the central processes of pseudounipolar neurons whose cell bodies lie in the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion. (2) Motor root—smaller root carrying special visceral efferent fibers that innervate the muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor palati, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric.

questions.text: Pain from the palatine tonsil is carried on the following cranial nerve:
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsil receives its general sensory innervation (pain, touch, temperature) from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), specifically through its tonsillar branch that innervates the mucosa over the tonsil. This explains why tonsillar pain may be referred to the ear via the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's nerve).
questions.keyConcept: Pain from palatine tonsil is carried by glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

questions.text: The glossopharyngeal nerve gives branches to:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) gives the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion (preganglionic parasympathetic for parotid gland), motor branches to the stylopharyngeus muscle, and sensory branches to the mucous membrane covering the palatine tonsil and posterior tongue. All three listed options are correct functions of CN IX.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX supplies otic ganglion, stylopharyngeus, and palatine tonsil mucosa.
options: The mucous membrane covering the tonsil.

questions.text: The glossopharyngeal nerve:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries special visceral afferent (taste) fibers from the posterior one-third of the tongue to the nucleus solitarius. It does NOT supply all pharyngeal muscles (only stylopharyngeus); the constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. It also does NOT pass superficial to hyoglossus (it passes between the superior and middle constrictors to reach the pharynx). Therefore, only statement B is correct.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX carries taste from posterior one-third of tongue; does NOT supply all pharyngeal muscles.
options: Carries taste sensation from posterior 1/3 of tongue.

questions.text: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the mucous membrane of:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the mucous membrane of the oropharynx, including the palatine tonsils and posterior one-third of the tongue. The nasopharynx is supplied by the maxillary nerve (V2) via the sphenopalatine ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal supplies oropharynx, not nasopharynx, laryngopharynx, or larynx.

questions.text: The hypoglossal nerve:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the skull through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen. It carries C1 spinal nerve fibers that branch off to supply the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles. CN XII does NOT lie within the carotid sheath (it crosses superficially over it), is NOT joined by C2, is purely motor (NOT sensory), and emerges between the pyramid and the olive (not between the olive and ICP).
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve carries C1 fibers and supplies thyrohyoid and geniohyoid; joined by branch from C1 not C2.
options: Emerges from medulla between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Leaves the skull through jugular foramen.
Lies within the upper part of carotid sheath.
Is joined by a branch from C2.
It sensory to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.

questions.text: As regards branches of glossopharyngeal nerve, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve has several branches: the tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) contributes to the lesser petrosal nerve for parotid secretion; the tonsillar and lingual branches carry sensation from the tonsil and posterior one-third of the tongue (including taste); the pharyngeal branch carries sensory and motor fibers to the pharyngeal plexus; and the muscular branch supplies the stylopharyngeus. However, taste from the anterior TWO-THIRDS of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani of the facial nerve (CN VII), not the glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior two-thirds tongue taste is CN VII (chorda tympani), NOT glossopharyngeal.
options: Its tympanic branch shares in providing nerve supply to parotid gland.
Its pharyngeal branch carries sensory fibers.
It gives a muscular branch to stylopharyngeus.
Its tonsillar branch supplies soft palate.
Its lingual branch carries special sensation from anterior 2/3 of tongue

questions.text: Enumerate branches of glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) has several branches: (1) tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) to the middle ear, forming the tympanic plexus; (2) lesser petrosal nerve (from tympanic plexus) to the otic ganglion for parotid gland secretion; (3) carotid branch (nerve of Hering) to the carotid body and carotid sinus; (4) pharyngeal branches contributing to the pharyngeal plexus; (5) tonsillar branches to the palatine tonsils; (6) lingual branches to the posterior one-third of the tongue (general sensation and taste); and (7) muscular branch to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX branches: tympanic, lesser petrosal, carotid, pharyngeal, tonsillar, lingual, and stylopharyngeus.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of glossopharyngeal nerve: (1) tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve); (2) lesser petrosal nerve (to otic ganglion); (3) carotid branch (nerve of Hering); (4) pharyngeal branches; (5) tonsillar branches; (6) lingual branches (posterior 1/3 tongue); (7) muscular branch to stylopharyngeus.

questions.text: Enumerate branches of hypoglossal nerve.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the hypoglossal canal above the occipital condyle, descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, and curves forward above the hyoid bone to reach the tongue. Its branches include: (1) meningeal branch to the dura of posterior cranial fossa; (2) descending hypoglossi (C1 fibers) contributing to the ansa cervicalis; (3) nerve to thyrohyoid (C1 fibers); (4) nerve to geniohyoid (C1 fibers); and (5) lingual branches to the muscles of the tongue (hyoglossus, genioglossus, styloglossus, and intrinsic tongue muscles).
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal branches: meningeal, C1 to ansa cervicalis, C1 to thyrohyoid/geniohyoid, lingual branches to tongue muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of hypoglossal nerve: (1) meningeal branch to posterior cranial fossa dura; (2) descending hypoglossi (C1 fibers to ansa cervicalis); (3) nerve to thyrohyoid (C1); (4) nerve to geniohyoid (C1); (5) lingual branches to all extrinsic and intrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus, superior/inferior longitudinal, transverse, vertical).

questions.text: The branchial arch supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve is the:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch. It supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle (the only muscle derived from the 3rd arch) and provides sensory innervation to the pharynx, middle ear, and posterior third of the tongue. CN V3 is 1st arch; CN VII is 2nd; CN X superior laryngeal is 4th.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the nerve of the 3rd pharyngeal arch.

questions.text: The pharyngeal arch supplied by the only pontine cranial nerve that is not attached to the lower border of the pons is the:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) is the only cranial nerve attached to the lower border of the pons (all others attach at the upper border). It supplies the lateral rectus muscle of the eye, derived from the 6th pharyngeal arch. The 1st arch nerve is CN V (trigeminal), which attaches to the upper pons.
questions.keyConcept: CN VI (abducent) is the only cranial nerve attached to the LOWER border of the pons; innervates lateral rectus (6th arch).

questions.text: Enumerate derivatives of the pharyngeal arch supplied by the facial nerve.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) is the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch. All muscles, cartilages, and bones derived from the second arch are supplied by CN VII. These include muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, and the styloid process of the hyoid bone.
questions.keyConcept: CN VII (facial nerve) supplies: muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, and styloid process.
questions.modelAnswer: Derivatives of the second pharyngeal arch supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII): (1) Muscles—muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric. (2) Bones—styloid process of hyoid bone and lesser horn of hyoid (via Reichert's cartilage). (3) Ligaments—stylohyoid ligament. All these structures are innervated by CN VII regardless of their final anatomical position.

questions.text: Which of the following nerves supplying the scalp and face is not derived from the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The greater occipital nerve (C2) is NOT derived from the trigeminal nerve - it's a dorsal ramus of C2.选项A正确. The answer is A. It supplies the scalp posterior to the auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve (C2 dorsal ramus) is the only scalp nerve not from trigeminal - supplies posterior scalp.

questions.text: The branch of facial nerve that supplies the platysma is the
questions.explanation: The branch of facial nerve that supplies the platysma is the cervical branch (also called mandibular branch in some texts).选项E正确. The answer is E. Platysma is a neck muscle of facial expression.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical branch of facial nerve supplies platysma - the only muscle in the neck from facial nerve.

questions.text: Special visceral efferent nuclei include:
questions.explanation: Special visceral efferent nuclei include: trigeminal motor nucleus (V), facial motor nucleus (VII), nucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI), and hypoglossal nucleus (XII).选项D正确. The answer is D. These innervate pharyngeal arch-derived muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Special visceral efferent nuclei: CN V, VII, IX, X, XI motor nuclei - innervate pharyngeal arch muscles.

questions.text: Injury of motor root of trigeminal nerve would cause paralysis of:
questions.explanation: Injury of motor root of trigeminal nerve (portio minor) would cause paralysis of: muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini.选项B正确. The answer is B. These are all innervated by CN V3 motor root.
questions.keyConcept: Motor root of CN V: mastication muscles, mylohyoid, digastric, tensor tympani/veli palatini - all affected.

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei receive the GSA fibers of facial nerve:
questions.explanation: GSA (general somatic afferent) fibers of the facial nerve carry proprioception from facial muscles and sensation from a small area of the external ear. These fibers relay in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, which spans the pons and medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve GSA: relays in spinal nucleus of trigeminal (same as other facial sensation).

questions.text: Cranial nerve nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle close to midline in lower pons is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle, close to the midline in the lower pons. It supplies the lateral rectus muscle. The facial motor nucleus is more lateral, and the hypoglossal nucleus is in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nucleus: floor of 4th ventricle, lower pons, near midline; supplies lateral rectus.

questions.text: The only cranial nerve that decussate before its emergence is:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the ONLY cranial nerve that decussates (crosses) before emerging from the brainstem. It decussates in the superior medullary velum. All other cranial nerves emerge without crossing.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV (trochlear): only cranial nerve that decussates before emergence; crosses in superior medullary velum.

questions.text: Cranial nerves in medulla oblongata are the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) emerges from the PONS (at pontomedullary junction), not the medulla. The medullary cranial nerves are: IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal).
questions.keyConcept: Medullary cranial nerves: CN IX, X, XI, XII. CN VII (facial) is pontine.

questions.text: Mention the cranial nerves present in the ventral surface of the medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: The cranial nerves with nuclei or roots in the medulla are CN IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal). They emerge from the posterolateral sulcus (IX, X, XI) and anterolateral sulcus (XII).
questions.keyConcept: Medullary cranial nerves: CN IX, X, XI (posterolateral sulcus), CN XII (anterolateral sulcus).
questions.modelAnswer: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), vagus nerve (CN X), accessory nerve (CN XI), and hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). They emerge from the posterolateral sulcus (CN IX, X, XI) and anterolateral sulcus (CN XII).

questions.text: Mention the cranial nerves present in the ventral surface of the pons.
questions.explanation: The cranial nerves present in the pons are CN V (trigeminal - pontine), VI (abducent - pontine), VII (facial - pontomedullary junction), and VIII (vestibulocochlear - pontomedullary junction). The facial and vestibulocochlear emerge at the cerebellopontine angle.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine cranial nerves: CN V, VI, VII, VIII. Trigeminal (lateral pons), abducent ( midline), facial/vestibulocochlear (cerebellopontine angle).
questions.modelAnswer: Trigeminal nerve (CN V), abducent nerve (CN VI), facial nerve (CN VII), and vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). They emerge from the pontine surface: trigeminal laterally, abducent at the midline, and facial/vestibulocochlear at the cerebellopontine angle.

questions.text: Mention the cranial nerve nuclei belonging to GSE column.
questions.explanation: The GSE (general somatic efferent) cranial nerve nuclei are: oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), abducent (CN VI), and hypoglossal (CN XII). These supply extraocular muscles and tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: GSE cranial nerve nuclei: CN III, IV, VI, XII. Supply extraocular and tongue muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: Nucleus of oculomotor nerve (CN III), nucleus of trochlear nerve (CN IV), nucleus of abducent nerve (CN VI), and nucleus of hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). These supply the extraocular muscles (except superior oblique and lateral rectus) and tongue muscles.

questions.text: Mention the cranial nerve nuclei belonging to SVE column and mention their distribution.
questions.explanation: The SVE (special visceral efferent) nuclei include: motor nucleus of CN V (muscles of mastication + tensor tympani/palate), motor nucleus of CN VII (facial muscles), and nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X, XI - pharynx/larynx muscles).
questions.keyConcept: SVE nuclei: motor V (mastication), motor VII (facial expression), nucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI - pharynx/larynx).
questions.modelAnswer: Motor nucleus of trigeminal (CN V): supplies muscles of first pharyngeal arch (masticatory muscles, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, anterior digastric). Motor nucleus of facial (CN VII): supplies muscles of second pharyngeal arch (facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric). Nucleus ambiguus: CN IX - stylopharyngeus; CN X and XI - muscles of palate, pharynx, and larynx.

questions.text: Mention the cranial nerve nuclei belonging to GVE column.
questions.explanation: The GVE (general visceral efferent) nuclei include: Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III - pupillary constriction), superior salivatory nucleus (CN VII - lacrimal and salivary glands), inferior salivatory nucleus (CN IX - parotid gland), and dorsal vagal nucleus (CN X - thoracic/abdominal viscera).
questions.keyConcept: GVE nuclei: Edinger-Westphal (III), superior salivatory (VII), inferior salivatory (IX), dorsal vagal (X).
questions.modelAnswer: Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III) - parasympathetic to eye (pupillary constriction, accommodation). Superior salivatory nucleus (CN VII) - submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, lacrimal gland. Inferior salivatory nucleus (CN IX) - parotid gland. Dorsal vagal nucleus (CN X) - parasympathetic to thoracic and abdominal viscera.

questions.text: Mention the branches of glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) gives off: tympanic branch (to middle ear and meninges), carotid branch (to carotid body and sinus), pharyngeal branches (to pharyngeal mucosa), muscular branch (to stylopharyngeus), tonsillar branches (to tonsil), and lingual branches (to posterior 1/3 of tongue).
questions.keyConcept: CN IX branches: tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular (stylopharyngeus), tonsillar, lingual.
questions.modelAnswer: Tympanic branch (to middle ear and mastoid air cells), carotid branch (to carotid sinus and body), pharyngeal branches (to pharyngeal mucosa), muscular branch (to stylopharyngeus muscle), tonsillar branches (to palatine tonsil), and lingual branches (to posterior 1/3 of tongue for taste and general sensation).

questions.text: Which of the following nerves supplying scalp and face Is not derived from trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) is derived from the cervical plexus, not the trigeminal nerve. It supplies the skin over the parotid gland and mastoid area. The auriculotemporal, zygomaticotemporal, supraorbital, and supratrochlear are all trigeminal branches.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve from C2-C3 cervical plexus, not trigeminal (V)

questions.text: The corticonuclear (corticobulbar) tract provides only contralateral innervation to which of the following cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The corticobulbar tract provides bilateral innervation to muscles of the head and face, EXCEPT for the lower facial muscles (chin, lips) which receive only contralateral input. This bilateral pattern preserves function if one hemisphere is damaged.
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar fibers to lower face are uniquely contralateral; all other cranial nerve motor nuclei receive bilateral input.

questions.text: A patient has a tumor in the fourth ventricle. Which cranial nerve nucleus is most likely affected due to its location?
questions.explanation: The abducens nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle, near the facial colliculus. A fourth ventricle tumor would most likely affect the abducens nerve, which has a long intracranial course.
questions.keyConcept: Abducens nucleus in the pons is vulnerable to fourth ventricle masses due to its dorsal location.

questions.text: Which cranial nerve emerges from the dorsal (back) aspect of the brainstem?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as it exits dorsally from the midbrain (just below the inferior colliculus) after decussating in the superior medullary velum. All other cranial nerves exit ventrally.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV is the only cranial nerve with dorsal exit from the midbrain after decussation.

questions.text: Which cranial nerve nuclei are located in the pons?
questions.explanation: Pontine cranial nerve nuclei include: abducens (VI), facial (VII), vestibulocochlear (VIII), and the principal sensory nucleus of trigeminal (V). The oculomotor and trochlear nuclei are in the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: CN V, VI, VII, VIII nuclei are located in the pons; III and IV are midbrain, IX, X, XI, XII are medullary.

questions.text: Which cranial nerve is not found in the open medulla?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) emerges from the pre-olivary sulcus of the closed medulla, not the open medulla. Cranial nerves IX, X, XI emerge from the open medulla at the post-olivary area.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII emerges from the closed medulla; CN IX, X, XI emerge from the open medulla.

questions.text: Which cranial nerve nucleus is located most medially in the medulla?
questions.explanation: The nucleus tractus solitarius (solitary nucleus) is located most medially in the medulla, receiving visceral sensory input from vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves for taste and visceral reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Solitary nucleus is the most medial medullary nucleus, involved in visceral sensory processing.

questions.text: Which cranial nerve nucleus contains both general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA) fibers?
questions.explanation: The nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla contains both GVA (visceral sensation including baroreceptor and chemoreceptor input) and SVA (taste) fibers, making it unique in having both modalities.
questions.keyConcept: Solitary nucleus processes both visceral afferent and special visceral afferent (taste) information.

questions.text: Which cranial nerve supplies fibers to the nucleus ambiguus?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides the parasympathetic and motor fibers to the nucleus ambiguus for innervation of the stylopharyngeus muscle. The nucleus ambiguus also receives contributions from CN X and XI.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus innervates pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles via CN IX, X, and XI.

questions.text: At which anatomical level does the oculomotor nerve emerge?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges from the midbrain on the anterior surface between the cerebral peduncles, just posterior to the posterior clinoid process.
questions.keyConcept: CN III emerges from the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles on the anterior surface.
options: At the level of the superior midbrain colliculus
At the level of the inferior olivary nucleus
At the level of the pons
At the level of the medullary pyramids
At the level of the cerebellar peduncles

questions.text: Which structure receives its sensory innervation from the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The dura mater receives sensory innervation from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve. The anterior cranial fossa is innervated by V1, the middle cranial fossa by V2 and V3.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater sensory innervation is provided by all three trigeminal divisions via meningeal branches.
options: Skin over the angle of the mandible

questions.text: Which nerve is the motor branch of the posterior division of the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid nerve is the motor branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3). It innervates the mylohyoid muscle and anterior belly of the digastric muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Mylohyoid nerve from V3 posterior division supplies mylohyoid and anterior digastric muscles.

questions.text: One of the following cranial nerves contains sensory nerves fibers:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) contains sensory fibers for face, scalp, and oral cavity; the other listed nerves are purely motor.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal sensory function

questions.text: One of the following cranial nerves is attached to the posterior aspect of the brain stem:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the posterior aspect of the brainstem, specifically from the dorsal surface of the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve origin

questions.text: Which cranial nerve emerges from the anterior aspect of the medulla oblongata between the pyramid and the olive?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the anterior aspect of the medulla between the pyramid and olive, carrying only motor fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve origin

questions.text: Cranial nerves on ventral pons:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves associated with the ventral pons include CN V (trigeminal), CN VI (abducent), CN VII (facial), and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear), emerging at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine cranial nerves: 5, 6, 7, 8.
questions.modelAnswer: Trigeminal (5), Abducent (6), Facial (7), Vestibulocochlear (8).

questions.text: Branches of glossopharyngeal nerve:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) gives six branches: tympanic (to middle ear), carotid (to carotid body/sinus), pharyngeal (to pharynx), muscular (to stylopharyngeus), tonsillar, and lingual branches.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX branches: tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar, lingual.
questions.modelAnswer: Tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar, lingual.

questions.text: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve belongs to which column of cranial nerve nuclei?
questions.explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is a special visceral efferent (SVE) nucleus, innervating muscles derived from the first pharyngeal arch (muscles of mastication).
questions.keyConcept: Motor nucleus of V is special visceral efferent (SVE).

questions.text: The optic nerve is a derivative of the:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve develops as an outpouching of the diencephalon (forerain), making it technically a CNS tract rather than a true peripheral nerve, with myelin provided by oligodendrocytes.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve is a diencephalon derivative, not true peripheral nerve.

questions.text: Which of the following is a pure motor cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is a pure motor nerve carrying general somatic efferent fibers to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, with no sensory component.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is pure motor to tongue muscles.

questions.text: The facial nerve leaves the cranial cavity by passing through:
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) exits the cranial cavity through the stylomastoid foramen located between the styloid and mastoid processes.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve exits via stylomastoid foramen.

questions.text: Facial nerve DOESN'T give parasympathetic supply to ……… gland.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve provides parasympathetic supply to the lacrimal gland via the greater petrosal nerve and to submandibular and sublingual glands via chorda tympani; the parotid gland receives parasympathetic from CN IX.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve doesn't parasympathetically supply parotid gland (CN IX does).

questions.text: The hypoglossal nerve pierces ……… muscle at the end of its course.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) pierces the genioglossus muscle near its insertion before distributing to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve pierces genioglossus muscle.

questions.text: Nerve attached to the lower border of pons above pyramid is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) is attached to the lower border of the pons, in the groove between the pons and pyramid of the medulla. It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve at lower pons above pyramid

questions.text: Medial eminence in floor of fourth ventricle overlies the nucleus of:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus in the floor of the fourth ventricle. The facial colliculus (a elevation) is formed by the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers looping around it.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus

questions.text: Brain stem includes all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The brain stem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum lies posterior to the brain stem and is not considered part of it, though it is connected by three peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellum not part of brain stem

questions.text: Which of the following nerves lies close to the median plane in the transverse furrow between pons and medulla?
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) emerges at the pontomedullary junction, close to the median plane (between the pons and pyramid). It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at this junction.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial at pontomedullary junction

questions.text: As regards medulla oblongata, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) lies MEDIAL to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Rootlets emerge between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The statement in option D incorrectly places it lateral to ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus nerve medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle
options: Olive lies just lateral to anterior median fissure.
Inferior cerebellar peduncle lies lateral to olive.
XII cranial nerve exits from medulla lateral to pyramid.
X cranial nerve lies medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle.
XI cranial nerve is attached to posterolateral sulcus.

questions.text: As regards pons, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: Cerebellopontine angle tumors typically arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve (acoustic neuroma/schwannoma) and cause hearing loss, vertigo, and later facial nerve involvement. Pontine gliomas would cause different symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: CPA tumors cause deafness and vertigo
options: Cerebello-pontine angle gives attachment to VI & VII cranial nerves.
Nervus intermedius is the medial root of the facial nerve.
VIII cranial nerve lies medial to VII cranial nerve.
Its ventral surface shows a sulcus for vertebral artery.

questions.text: In dorsal surface of medulla oblongata, choose CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The vestibular trigone lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea in the floor of the fourth ventricle. This is the correct statement about dorsal medullary surface features.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular trigone between limbs of inferior fovea
options: Gracile tubercle is the most medial structure of open medulla.
Base of open medulla is formed by medullary stria.
Vestibular trigone lies between limbs of inferior fovea.
Hypoglossal trigone forms most medial trigone of superior fovea.
Apex of open medulla is continuous with cerebral aqueduct.

questions.text: As regards back of pons, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus, not the facial nucleus. The facial nucleus lies more laterally and is overlain by the facial colliculus formed by fibers wrapping around the abducent nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus, not facial
options: Its apex is continuous with cerebral acqueduct.
Locus ceruleus lies at upper end of sulcus limitans.
Sulcus limitans lies lateral to medial eminence.
Vestibular area lies lateral to superior fovea.

questions.text: A collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem form:
questions.explanation: A lemniscus is a collection of sensory fibers that ascend through the brainstem. Examples include the medial lemniscus (fine touch/proprioception), spinal lemniscus (pain/temperature), and trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation).
questions.keyConcept: Lemniscus is collection of ascending fibers in brainstem

questions.text: Which one of the following is an afferent connection to the inferior colliculus:
questions.explanation: This matching tests midbrain structures: cerebral aqueduct (around which the tectal plate curves); trochlear nucleus (inferior to oculomotor); superior cerebellar peduncle (lateral to red nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in midbrain

questions.text: Which one of the following decussations is associated with red nucleus?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the motor nucleus supplying muscles of the larynx (and pharynx/soft palate). It is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI for these muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus supplies laryngeal muscles
options: Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.text: As regards the internal structure of the midbrain, choose the CORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It supplies stylopharyngeus (IX), pharynx/larynx muscles (X), and sternocleidomastoid/trapezius (XI).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus - common motor for IX, X, XI
options: Parieto-pontine fibers - medial 1/5 of crus cerebri.
Ventral tegmental Decussation - tegmentum at level of inferior colliculus.
Cortico-spinal tract - lateral 1/5 of crus cerebri.
Cortico-nuclear tract - middle 3/5 of crus cerebri.

questions.text: Tegmentum pontis contains all the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve is the inferior salivary nucleus. It provides parasympathetic innervation to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior salivary nucleus - parasympathetic to parotid

questions.text: For each structure in left column, choose its appropriate place in midbrain from right column:
questions.explanation: The somatic efferent column includes: oculomotor nucleus (III), trochlear nucleus (IV), abducent nucleus (VI), and hypoglossal nucleus (XII). These nuclei supply muscles derived from somites.
questions.keyConcept: CN III, IV, VI, XII are somatic efferent nuclei

pairs.target: d. Area between crus cerebri & tegmentum.

questions.text: Regarding the medulla oblongata, the medial zone containing the pyramid is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The medial zone of the medulla (containing the pyramid) is supplied by the anterior spinal artery, which runs in the anterior median fissure. The lateral and posterior regions are supplied by vertebral artery branches and PICA.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal supplies medial medulla/pyramid

questions.text: Describe dorsal surface of medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: The dorsal surface of the medulla oblongata shows: (1) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - connects medulla to cerebellum; (2) MIDDLE CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - visible at the pontomedullary junction; (3) FLOOR OF FOURTH VENTRICLE: divided into MEDULLARY TRIGONE (containing hypoglossal trigone over hypoglossal nucleus and vagal trigone over dorsal motor nucleus of X) and PONTINE TRIGONE. The gracile and cuneate tubercles (over dorsal column nuclei) are visible above the trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal medulla: inferior/middle cerebellar peduncles, hypoglossal and vagal trigones in fourth ventricle floor
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI IN MEDULLA: (SOMATIC EFFERENT) Hypoglossal nucleus; (VISCERAL EFFERENT) Dorsal motor nucleus of X, inferior salivary nucleus; (VISCERAL AFFERENT) Nucleus solitarius; (TRIGEMINAL) Spinal nucleus of V; (AUDITORY) Cochlear nuclei; (VESTIBULAR) Vestibular nuclei; (OTHER) Olivary nuclei, cuneate/gracile nuclei, accessory cuneate nucleus.

questions.text: Describe dorsal surface of pons.
questions.explanation: The dorsal surface of the pons forms the upper part of the floor of the fourth ventricle: (1) FACIAL COLLICULUS - elevation over abducens nucleus and facial nerve fibers internally; (2) TRIGEMINAL TUBERCLE - over the principal sensory nucleus of CN V; (3) MEDIAL EMINENCE - longitudinal elevation; (4) SUPERIOR and INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLES form the lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle at this level.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal pons: facial colliculus, trigeminal tubercle, forms upper fourth ventricle floor with peduncles as lateral borders
questions.modelAnswer: INFERIOR OLIVARY COMPLEX: (COMPONENTS) Main olivary nucleus (folded gray matter), medial accessory olivary nucleus, dorsal accessory olivary nucleus; (CONNECTIONS) Receives input from red nucleus, spinal cord, and cerebral cortex; (OUTPUT) Olivocerebellar fibers cross and enter cerebellum via inferior cerebellar peduncle; (FUNCTION) Involved in motor learning and coordination.

questions.text: Enumerate internal features of medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: Internal features of the medulla oblongata include: (1) PYRAMIDS - containing corticospinal fibers, located on either side of anterior median fissure; (2) OLVES - containing inferior olivary nuclei; (3) INTERNAL ARCUATE FIBERS - decussating sensory fibers from dorsal column nuclei; (4) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS - formed after sensory decussation, ascends through brainstem; (5) CRANIAL NERVE NUCLEI: hypoglossal, dorsal motor nucleus of X, nucleus solitarius, nucleus ambiguus, inferior salivary nucleus; (6) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLES laterally.
questions.keyConcept: Medulla internal features: pyramids, olives, internal arcuate fibers, medial lemniscus, cranial nerve nuclei
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL NERVE: (1) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (SVE) - motor to stylopharyngeus muscle; (2) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to parotid gland via otic ganglion; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA/GVA) - taste from posterior 1/3 of tongue and visceral sensation; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (GSA) - general sensation from middle ear, pharynx.

questions.text: Describe pyramidal decussation.
questions.explanation: Pyramidal decussation: LOCATION at the caudal medulla where the medulla transitions to the spinal cord. PROCESS: About 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross obliquely in the anterior median fissure. RESULT: Crossed fibers form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral white column; uncrossed fibers remain as the anterior corticospinal tract. CLINICAL: This decussation explains why unilateral cerebral lesions cause contralateral motor deficits.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal decussation: 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross at caudal medulla to form lateral CST
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF FACIAL NERVE: (1) FACIAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (SVE) - motor to muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric; (2) SUPERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA) - taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue; (4) MESENCEPHALIC NUCLEUS OF V - proprioception from facial muscles.

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei in medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: Nuclei in the medulla oblongata include: (1) HYPOGLOSSAL NUCLEUS (somatic efferent) - in floor near central canal, supplies tongue muscles; (2) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS OF X (visceral efferent) - parasympathetic to thoracic/abdominal viscera; (3) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (special visceral efferent) - motor to pharynx/larynx; (4) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (visceral efferent) - parasympathetic to parotid; (5) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (visceral afferent) - taste and general visceral sensation; (6) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (general somatic afferent); (7) COCHLEAR and VESTIBULAR NUCLEI; (8) GRACILE and CUNEATE NUCLEI; (9) ACCESSORY CUNEATE NUCLEUS.
questions.keyConcept: Medullary nuclei: hypoglossal, dorsal motor X, nucleus ambiguus, inferior salivary, nucleus solitarius, cochlear/vestibular nuclei
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF OCULOMOTOR NERVE: (1) OCULOMOTOR NUCLEUS (SSE) - motor to superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique muscles; (2) EDINGER-WESTPHAL NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to sphincter pupillae (pupil constriction) and ciliary muscle (accommodation); (3) Central caudal nucleus - coordinates function.

questions.text: Enumerate structures in tegmentum pontis.
questions.explanation: Structures in the tegmentum pontis include: (1) CRANIAL NERVE NUCLEI: Abducens nucleus (CN VI), Facial nucleus (CN VII), Vestibular nuclei (CN VIII), Cochlear nuclei (CN VIII); (2) TRACT: Medial longitudinal fasciculus; (3) LEMNISCI: Medial lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus; (4) NUCLEI: Superior olivary nucleus (sound localization), nuclei of reticular formation; (5) TRAPEZOID BODY (auditory pathway); (6) The pyramid does NOT continue here (interrupted by transverse pontocerebellar fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Tegmentum pontis: CN VI, VII, VIII nuclei, medial lemniscus, superior olivary nucleus, reticular formation
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GVE COLUMN: (1) EDINGER-WESTPHAL NUCLEUS (III) - ciliary and pterygopalatine ganglia (eye, lacrimal); (2) SUPERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (VII) - submandibular and sublingual glands; (3) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (IX) - otic ganglion to parotid; (4) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS OF X - thoracic and abdominal viscera.

questions.text: Describe parts of midbrain & enumerate structures within each part.
questions.explanation: The midbrain has three parts: (1) TECTUM (quadrigeminal plate) - dorsal, contains superior colliculus (visual reflexes) and inferior colliculus (auditory relay); (2) TEGMENTUM - between tectum and crus cerebri, contains crus cerebri, substantia nigra, red nucleus, RAPPORT decussation, medial lemniscus, and decussations of superior cerebellar peduncle and red nucleus; (3) CRUS CEREBRI (cerebral peduncle) - ventral, contains descending motor fibers (frontopontine most medial, corticospinal/corticobulbar middle, parieto/temporopontine most lateral).
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain parts: tectum (colliculi), tegmentum (red nucleus, substantia nigra), crus cerebri (descending fibers)
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GSA COLUMN: (1) TRIGEMINAL NUCLEI (principal and spinal) - face, head; (2) COCHLEAR NUCLEI - hearing; (3) VESTIBULAR NUCLEI - balance; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V - general sensation from head and face. All receive general somatic afferent fibers from head and neck region.

questions.text: Enumerate tegmental decussations of midbrain.
questions.explanation: Tegmental decussations of the midbrain include: (1) DECUSSATION OF SUPERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - dentate nucleus output to thalamus crosses in midbrain; (2) DECUSSATION OF RED NUCLEUS (rubrobulbar and rubospinal tracts) - crosses just below superior colliculus; (3) TROCHLEAR NERVE DECUSSATION - CN IV is unique as the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally and completely cross before emerging. These decussations are part of the extrapyramidal motor system.
questions.keyConcept: Tegmental decussations: superior cerebellar peduncle, red nucleus, and trochlear nerve (only dorsal-exiting CN)
questions.modelAnswer: MEDIAL MEDULLARY SYNDROME: (CAUSE) Occlusion of anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery; (SIGNS) IPSILATERAL: tongue paralysis (hypoglossal nerve); CONTRALATERAL: UMN paralysis of body (pyramidal tract), loss of proprioception and fine touch (medial lemniscus); (PRESERVED) Pain and temperature (spinothalamic intact), dorsal column for upper levels.

questions.text: Describe the arterial supply of medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale gives passage to emissary veins connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid plexus of veins. This provides a route for infection spread from face to meninges.
questions.keyConcept: Foramen ovale has emissary veins of cavernous sinus
questions.modelAnswer: ARTERIAL SUPPLY OF MEDULLA: (1) ANTERIOR SPINAL ARTERY → supplies medial medulla (pyramids, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal nucleus) - thrombosis causes medial medullary syndrome; (2) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES → supply lateral surfaces; (3) POSTERIOR INFERIOR CEREBELLAR ARTERY (PICA) → supplies lateral medulla (olive, inferior cerebellar peduncle, vestibular/cochlear nuclei) - thrombosis causes lateral medullary syndrome; (4) Direct medullary branches from vertebral arteries.

questions.text: A 30-year-old patient comes to the emergency room with a laceration on the scalp following a head injury. The wound appears to be bleeding profusely. Which layer of the scalp is primarily responsible for this bleeding?
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of the scalp is highly vascular because it contains the arteries and veins of the scalp embedded in a firm fatty layer. This layer has rich anastomoses between the supraorbital, superficial temporal, and occipital arteries. The skin containsplexuses but the profuse bleeding in scalp lacerations is mainly from this highly vascular subcutaneous layer. The galea'subgaleal layer is avascular and the pericranium is thin.
questions.keyConcept: Subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of scalp is highly vascular; main source of profuse bleeding in scalp injuries due to arterial anastomoses.

questions.text: A patient presents with a complaint of persistent numbness and tingling on the posterior aspect of their scalp, especially on the left side behind the ear. They report no other neurological symptoms. Which nerve is likely responsible for this sensation?
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus (C2) that supplies the skin of the scalp posterior to the ear and the upper part of the lateral surface of the auricle. The greater occipital nerve (C2) supplies the posterior scalp near the midline. The posterior auricular nerve (branch of CN VII) supplies behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the scalp posterior and lateral to the ear (posterolateral scalp).

questions.text: Which part of the spinal cord is responsible for transmitting motor signals to the muscles that control fine movements of the fingers and hands?
questions.explanation: Fine movements of the fingers and hands are controlled by the C8-T1 spinal cord segments, which give rise to the ulnar and median nerves. The cervical region of the spinal cord (C5-T1) is enlarged at the cervicothoracic junction (intumescence) specifically to accommodate the large number of motor neurons for the upper limbs. The lumbar region controls the lower limbs.
questions.keyConcept: Finger/hand fine movements = CERVICAL spinal cord region (especially C8-T1); cervical enlargement supplies upper limb nerves.

questions.text: A 44-year-old female patient has a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle in the midbrain. She would present with a loss of:
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract decussates at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla. After decussation, the fibers descend in the lateral column of the spinal cord. A right cerebral peduncle lesion affects fibers that have NOT yet decussated, therefore causing CONTRALATERAL (left-sided) motor weakness. The corticospinal fibers to the lower limb are most medial in the peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle contains corticospinal fibers BEFORE their decussation in the medulla; right peduncle lesion = LEFT-sided weakness.
options: fine touch and pain sensation from the entire left side of the body
fine touch and pain sensation from the entire right side of the body
skeletal motor control to the entire right side of the body
skeletal motor control to both sides of the body
skeletal motor control to the entire left side of the body

questions.text: The facial colliculus overlies:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus overlies the abducens nucleus (CN VI) and internal genu of facial nerve - located on the floor of the 4th ventricle in the pons.选项E正确. The answer is E. It's a bulge caused by these nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus: overlies abducens nucleus and facial nerve genu - floor of fourth ventricle in pons.

questions.text: The superior colliculus of midbrain is formed of the following EXCEPT.
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus has 4 layers (stratum zonale, stratum cinereum, stratum opticum, stratum lemnisci), not 5. The stratum basilare (basal layer) is not a recognized layer of the superior colliculus. It is part of the visual reflex pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus layers (superficial to deep): zonale → cinereum → opticum → lemnisci. Not stratum basilare.

questions.text: Superior colliculus, all true except:
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus is NOT directly connected to the occipital cortex - that connection is via the visual cortex and lateral geniculate body. The superior colliculus is connected to the retina (via retinal ganglion cells), and gives rise to the tectospinal tract and dorsal tegmental decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus: connected to retina, not occipital cortex; gives tectospinal and dorsal tegmental decussation.
options: Give tectospinal tract & dorsal tegmental decussation.
Present in tectum of the upper midbrain.

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei extend in the midbrain:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve extends through the midbrain (alongside the central gray). It is the only sensory nucleus that contains primary afferent cell bodies. Vestibular nuclei are in the pons/medulla. Motor facial is pontine. Superior olive is pontine.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus of V: only primary afferent neuron in CNS, extends through midbrain.

questions.text: Which of the following tracts are present in the tegmentum pontis?
questions.explanation: The tegmentum pontis (pontine tegmentum) contains all of these: medial longitudinal fasciculus (vestibulo-ocular), spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature), and central tegmental tract (red nucleus to inferior olive).
questions.keyConcept: Pontine tegmentum: MLF, spinothalamic, central tegmental tracts. Basis pontis: corticospinal, transverse pontine fibers.

questions.text: Mention 3 external features of the ventral surface of the medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: The three main external features of the ventral medulla are: the pyramid (corticospinal tracts), olive (inferior olivary nucleus), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (lateral surface). The pyramids are visible as two longitudinal prominences on the anterior surface.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral medulla features: pyramid (motor), olive (olivary nucleus), ICP (lateral).
questions.modelAnswer: Pyramid (containing corticospinal tracts), olive (containing inferior olivary nucleus), and inferior cerebellar peduncle. These are visible on the ventral surface as longitudinal prominences on either side of the anterior median fissure.

questions.text: Mention the 3 elevations of the closed medulla (lower part of the back of medulla oblongata).
questions.explanation: The three elevations seen on the posterior surface of the lower closed medulla are the gracile tubercle (medial, for lower limb), cuneate tubercle (lateral, for upper limb), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (forming the lateral boundary). These overlie the respective nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior medulla elevations: gracile tubercle, cuneate tubercle, ICP. Correspond to dorsal column nuclei.
questions.modelAnswer: Gracile tubercle (medial, contains gracile nucleus for lower limb proprioception), cuneate tubercle (lateral, contains cuneate nucleus for upper limb proprioception), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (forms the posterolateral boundary of the medulla).

questions.text: What are the external features of the back of midbrain?
questions.explanation: The posterior surface of the midbrain shows the corpora quadrigemina - two superior colliculi (visual reflexes) and two inferior colliculi (auditory relay). These are separated by a cross-shaped sulcus. The cerebral peduncles are visible ventrally.
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain posterior features: 4 colliculi (2 superior, 2 inferior) - visual and auditory centers.
questions.modelAnswer: Four colliculi: two superior colliculi (visual reflexes - part of visual pathway, coordinates head/eye movements) and two inferior colliculi (auditory relay - part of lateral lemniscus pathway). They form the quadrigeminal plate separated by a cruciform sulcus.

questions.text: What forms the floor of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The floor of the fourth ventricle has two parts: pontine part (upper) showing medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area; and medullary part (lower) showing hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle floor: pontine = eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area; medullary = hypoglossal/vagal/vestibular trigones.
questions.modelAnswer: Pontine part: medial eminence, facial colliculus (CN VI nucleus with CN VII fibers), and vestibular area (vestibular nuclei). Medullary part: hypoglossal trigone (over hypoglossal nucleus), vagal trigone (over dorsal vagal nucleus), and vestibular trigone (vestibular nuclei).

questions.text: Mention the arteries that supply the pons.
questions.explanation: The pons is supplied by branches of the basilar artery, which runs in the basilar groove on the anterior surface. These include pontine arteries that penetrate the pons to supply the pontine nuclei and tegmentum.
questions.keyConcept: Pons: supplied by branches of basilar artery. Multiple pontine arteries penetrate the pons.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of the basilar artery. The basilar artery gives off numerous pontine arteries that supply the pons, including the basilar artery itself running in the basilar groove on the anterior surface.

questions.text: Mention the arteries that supply the midbrain.
questions.explanation: The midbrain is supplied by branches from the posterior cerebral artery (main supply to the cerebral peduncles and colliculi) and the superior cerebellar artery (supplying the inferior colliculus and surrounding area).
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain: branches of posterior cerebral artery and superior cerebellar artery.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of the posterior cerebral artery (supplies cerebral peduncles, red nucleus, substantia nigra, superior colliculus) and branches of the superior cerebellar artery (supplies inferior colliculus and adjacent midbrain).

questions.text: Hind brain (Rhombencephalon) includes the following Except
questions.explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; the crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (mesencephalon), not hindbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Hindbrain components

questions.text: Brain stem includes the following Except
questions.explanation: The brain stem includes midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata; the cerebellum and cerebral aqueduct are not part of the brain stem proper (cerebral aqueduct connects third and fourth ventricles).
questions.keyConcept: Brain stem structural components

questions.text: Proprioceptive sensation from the big toe ascends to the brainstem through which fibers?
questions.explanation: Proprioception from the lower limb ascends via the gracile fasciculus in the posterior columns to the gracile nucleus in the medulla, then decussates as internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile fasciculus carries lower limb proprioception to the medulla before decussation.

questions.text: Head rotation in response to visual stimuli, with crossing at the level of the superior colliculus, is mediated by which tract?
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract decussates at the superior medullary velum (rostral medulla), which is at the level of the midbrain-pons junction, not the midbrain itself.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract decussates at the level of the inferior colliculus/superior medullary velum.

questions.text: Decussation at the level of the superior midbrain occurs in which of the following tracts?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique in that it exits the midbrain dorsally and decussates completely before emerging. The oculomotor nerve exits ventrally. Other cranial nerves exit at pontine or medullary levels.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV is the only cranial nerve that decussates and exits dorsally from the midbrain.

questions.text: Which artery and its branches are primarily responsible for supplying the pons?
questions.explanation: The basilar artery and its branches (paramedian and circumferential pontine arteries) supply the pons. The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the anteroinferior pons, while superior cerebellar artery supplies the upper pons.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar artery supplies pons through paramedian and circumferential branches.

questions.text: Which of the following is present in the dorsal surface of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The corpora quadrigemina (superior and inferior colliculi) are on the dorsal midbrain surface. The basis pedunculi (cerebral peduncles) are on the ventral surface.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal midbrain features include the four colliculi (corpora quadrigemina) for visual and auditory reflexes.

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei, located in the midbrain, contains general visceral efferent (GVE) fibers?
questions.explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus (accessory oculomotor nucleus) is located in the midbrain and contains preganglionic parasympathetic neurons that supply the ciliary and sphincter pupillae muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to intraocular muscles.

questions.text: Which of the following arteries supplies the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The midbrain is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and its branches, including the posterior communicating artery. The basilar artery supplies the upper midbrain through its superior cerebellar artery branch.
questions.keyConcept: PCA and basilar artery branches supply the midbrain via posterior circulation.

questions.text: Which muscle is responsible for retraction of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The masseter muscle retracts the mandible (pulls it posteriorly). The temporalis also retracts, while the medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid (lower head) protract the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Masseter is the primary mandibular retractor; temporalis assists with retrusion.

questions.text: Ascending sensory bundle in brain stem, end in diencephalon:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus is an ascending sensory bundle in the brainstem carrying fine touch and proprioception information, terminating in the VPL nucleus of thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial lemniscus

questions.text: In lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) the lesion is in one of the following arteries:
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) results from PICA infarction, causing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ataxia, and hoarseness.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome

questions.text: Which tract is responsible for spino‑visual reflexes (turning the head and eyes toward a cutaneous stimulus)?
questions.explanation: The spinotectal tract carries pain information to the superior colliculus for reflex head and eye movements toward cutaneous stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Spinotectal reflex

questions.text: Which structure is present at the level of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract (carrying pallidal and cerebellar projections) is present at midbrain level, running between red nucleus and inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain structures

questions.text: A patient with a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle (midbrain) would present with:
questions.explanation: Right cerebral peduncle lesion causes left-sided motor weakness (contralateral) because corticospinal fibers have already crossed at the pyramidal decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle lesion
options: Loss of fine touch on the left side of the body
Loss of pain sensation on the right side
Skeletal motor loss on the entire left side

questions.text: External features of back of midbrain:
questions.explanation: The posterior midbrain displays four colliculi: two superior colliculi (involved in visual reflexes) and two inferior colliculi (involved in auditory reflexes), collectively forming the tectal plate or quadrigeminal plate.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior midbrain: two superior and two inferior colliculi.
questions.modelAnswer: 2 superior and 2 inferior colliculi.

questions.text: Floor of fourth ventricle:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle floor has two parts: the pontine part contains the medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area; the medullary part contains the hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of fourth ventricle: pontine (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area) and medullary (three trigones).
questions.modelAnswer: Pontine part (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area); Medullary part (hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, vestibular trigone).

questions.text: Arteries supplying pons:
questions.explanation: The pons is primarily supplied by paramedian and circumferential branches of the basilar artery, which penetrate the ventral surface to supply pontine nuclei and fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Pons supplied by branches of basilar artery.
questions.modelAnswer: The arteries supplying the pons include: (1) Basilar artery (main supply) — gives off pontine arteries; (2) Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) — from basilar, supplies lateral pons and middle cerebellar peduncle; (3) Superior cerebellar artery (SCA) — from basilar, supplies the upper pons.

questions.text: Arteries supplying midbrain:
questions.explanation: The midbrain receives blood from branches of the posterior cerebral artery (supplying the anterior and lateral regions) and branches of the superior cerebellar artery (supplying the posterior region).
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain supplied by posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar.

questions.text: Medial medullary syndrome causes:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery) causes contralateral spastic hemiplegia below the lesion, contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, and ipsilateral flaccid tongue paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiplegia, proprioception loss, ipsilateral tongue palsy.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral hemiplegia (flaccid), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, ipsilateral LMNL of tongue.

questions.text: Lateral medullary syndrome causes:
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome from PICA occlusion) causes ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, hoarseness, and Horner syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome: ipsilateral face, contralateral body sensory loss, ataxia, Horner syndrome.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral loss of pain/temp from face, contralateral loss from body, ipsilateral paralysis of palate/pharynx/larynx, loss of taste, ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome.

questions.text: Which nerve is responsible for the sensory innervation of the lower eyelid?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of V2) provides sensory innervation to the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, entering through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower eyelid sensory innervation: infraorbital nerve (V2).

questions.text: A tumor in the floor of the fourth ventricle (facial colliculus region) most directly damages which nucleus?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus in the floor of the 4th ventricle overlies the abducent (CN VI) nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus: facial nerve wraps around abducens nucleus in floor of fourth ventricle.

questions.text: Corticonuclear fibers pass through ……… of internal capsule to reach the brain stem.
questions.explanation: Corticonuclear fibers (corticobulbar tract) pass through the genu (bend) of the internal capsule to reach brainstem cranial nerve nuclei for voluntary control of face and neck muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Corticonuclear fibers pass through genu of internal capsule.

questions.text: Which one of the following ends in the VPMN of the thalamus?
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius (solitary nucleus) is the visceral afferent nucleus receiving general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA - taste) fibers from CN VII, IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius - visceral afferent column

questions.text: Nucleus ventralis posterior of thalamus receives the following Except:
questions.explanation: Nucleus ventralis posterior (VP) of the thalamus receives medial lemniscus (body tactile/proprioceptive), spinal lemniscus (body pain/temperature), trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation), and fibers from nucleus solitarius (gustatory). The lateral lemniscus carries auditory information to the inferior colliculus, NOT to VP nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: VP nucleus receives medial lemniscus, spinal lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus, and gustatory fibers; lateral lemniscus goes to inferior colliculus.

questions.text: Nucleus ventralis posterior medialis (VPM) of thalamus receives:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus receives the trigeminal lemniscus carrying pain, temperature, and touch sensation from the face and head. It also receives gustatory fibers from the nucleus solitarius. The medial lemniscus and spinal lemniscus terminate in VPL, not VPM.
questions.keyConcept: VPM receives trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation) and gustatory fibers from nucleus solitarius.

questions.text: The thalamic nucleus for pain and temperature sensations of head is:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus is the specific relay center for pain, temperature, and crude touch sensations from the head (face, scalp, meninges, and oral cavity). It receives input from the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve via the trigeminal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: VPM nucleus relays pain and temperature sensations specifically from the HEAD via trigeminal lemniscus.

questions.text: The thalamic nucleus in which spinal & medial lemnisci terminate is:
questions.explanation: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus is the thalamic relay for somatosensory information from the body. Both the medial lemniscus (carrying fine touch and proprioception from the body) and the spinal lemniscus (carrying pain and temperature from the body) terminate in the VPL nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: VPL nucleus is where spinal lemniscus (pain/temp from body) and medial lemniscus (touch/proprioception from body) terminate.

questions.text: Sensations received by the thalamus include all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The thalamus acts as a relay station for almost all sensory modalities (except olfaction) on their way to the cerebral cortex. It receives exteroceptive, proprioceptive, gustatory, visual, and auditory sensations. Olfaction (smell) is the only sensory modality that does not relay through the thalamus—olfactory signals go directly to the olfactory bulb and limbic system.
questions.keyConcept: All major sensations relay through thalamus EXCEPT smell; olfactory pathway bypasses thalamus to limbic system.

questions.text: Describe lateral part of thalamus & its nuclei.
questions.explanation: The lateral part of the thalamus is the largest portion and contains several nuclei. It includes the ventral tier nuclei (VA, VL, VP, VPL, VPM), the lateral nuclear group (lateral dorsal, lateral posterior, pulvinar), and the dorsal tier. These nuclei relay specific types of sensory and motor information to their respective cortical areas.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral thalamus: ventral tier nuclei (motor/sensory relay) and lateral nuclear group (LD, LP, pulvinar).
questions.modelAnswer: The lateral part of the thalamus is divided into ventral and dorsal tiers. Ventral tier nuclei: (1) Ventral anterior (VA) nucleus—motor relay from basal ganglia to premotor cortex. (2) Ventral lateral (VL) nucleus—motor relay from cerebellum and basal ganglia to motor cortex. (3) Ventral posterior (VP) nucleus—sensory relay; subdivided into VPL (receives body sensation via medial and spinal lemnisci) and VPM (receives head sensation via trigeminal lemniscus). Dorsal tier nuclei: (4) Lateral dorsal (LD) nucleus—projects to parietal cortex. (5) Lateral posterior (LP) nucleus—associated with pulvinar. (6) Pulvinar—the largest nucleus, projects to parietal, occipital, and temporal association cortices, involved in integrating sensory information.

questions.text: Sensations received by the thalamus are Except:
questions.explanation: The thalamus receives exteroceptive, proprioceptive, gustatory, visual, and auditory sensations but NOT smell (olfactory). Olfaction is the only special sense that does not relay through the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamus acts as sensory relay station for all senses except olfaction.

questions.text: The neocerebellum is anatomically located in the following part of the cerebellum:
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum (lateral parts of posterior lobe) is anatomically located in the posterior lobe of the cerebellum. It is concerned with planning and executing voluntary movements, particularly those requiring skilled precision.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellum in posterior lobe

questions.text: Thrombosis of posterior inferior cerebellar artery affects:
questions.explanation: PICA thrombosis causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: ipsilateral vestibular dysfunction (vertigo, nystagmus), cerebellar ataxia, facial pain/temperature loss, dysphagia, hoarseness, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss.
questions.keyConcept: PICA thrombosis causes lateral medullary syndrome

questions.text: What are the four tracts that carry unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The four tracts carrying unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum are: posterior spinocerebellar (lower limb, from Clarke's column), anterior spinocerebellar (both limbs, from spinal border cells), spino-olivary (to inferior olive then cerebellum), and cuneocerebellar (upper limb, from accessory cuneate nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum: posterior and anterior spinocerebellar, spino-olivary, cuneocerebellar tracts.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's column, lower limb). 2) Anterior spinocerebellar tract (from spinal border cells, both limbs). 3) Spino-olivary tract (to inferior olivary nucleus, then to cerebellum). 4) Cuneocerebellar tract (from accessory cuneate nucleus, upper limb).

questions.text: What is the neocerebellum formed of?
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum consists of the lateral parts of the cerebellar hemispheres (the largest part in humans). It receives cortical input via the pontocerebellar pathway and is involved in planning and executing voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellum: lateral cerebellar hemispheres. Receives cortical input, plans skilled movements.
questions.modelAnswer: The lateral parts of the cerebellar hemisphere. This is the phylogenetically newest part (neocerebellum), connected to the cerebral cortex via the pontocerebellar pathway, and involved in planning and execution of skilled voluntary movements.
